commentaries: Harold Bloom mentions Frye's critical interpretation of The Merchant of Venice as a Christian allegory, which he disputes.
Harold Bloom references Northrop Frye's critical interpretation of Dickens's work, summarizing his view on the thematic core of Dickens's novels.
Harold Bloom mentions the late critic Northrop Frye as an example of a canonical idealizer.
Northrop Frye comments that Gertrude Stein's prose uses repetition in a way that mimics musical capacity.
Harold Bloom cites Gertrude Stein's idea about writing for oneself and strangers, extending it to reading.
Northrop Frye lists several theorists, including Fergusson, whose books are cited as exceptionally useful for the archetypal approach in criticism.

Northrop Frye references Poe's essay 'The Poetic Principle' to illustrate a manifesto of the ironic age, which argues that poetry is oracular and discontinuous, and that epic verse is composed of lyrical passages connected by versified prose.
Northrop Frye mentions Poe's 'Bells' as part of the historical lineage of a tendency to ragtime in English poetry.
Northrop Frye references Poe's theories as part of a discontinuous approach to literary structure, which is reconciled with holistic views in a critical principle derived from examining the Bible.
Northrop Frye mentions Freud as part of a modern intellectual age whose ideas challenge the critical axioms assumed by Arnold.
Northrop Frye discusses Freud's analysis of Oedipus Tyrannus, noting how it links dramatic and psychological elements without relying on the playwright's personal life.
Northrop Frye mentions Freud in the context of psychological quests that involve redeemed paternal figures.
Northrop Frye references Freud's theoretical concept of wit, using it to explain the humorous and impulsive nature of puns in poetic creation.
Northrop Frye states that the dream-like work 'Finnegans Wake' utilizes the psychological research of Freud and Jung on dream mechanisms and wit.
Northrop Frye cites Freud's analysis of dream mechanisms as analogous to the creative process of fitting words into poetic patterns.
Northrop Frye references Freud's psychological concept of the Oedipus complex, suggesting it may actually be informed by the older myth of Oedipus, rather than explaining the myth.
Harold Bloom mentions Freud in the context of a chapter in the book, advocating for a Shakespearean interpretation of Freud's work.
Harold Bloom references Freud as a thinker whose key ideas are prefigured and critiqued within Shakespeare's works, suggesting Shakespeare's conceptual superiority.
Harold Bloom references Freud as a pivotal, canonical figure marking an endpoint in a long literary and intellectual tradition.
Harold Bloom references Freud as a figure whose cognitive negations provide strength to open up the canon.
Harold Bloom cites Freud as a sage whose thought has been shaped by Shakespeare's insights.
Harold Bloom references Sigmund Freud's belief in the Oxfordian theory of Shakespearean authorship.
Harold Bloom references Freud as a thinker who regarded Shakespeare's works as culturally central.
Harold Bloom critiques Freud's interpretation of King Lear, specifically referencing Freud's essay 'Theme of the Three Caskets' where Freud identifies Cordelia with Death.
Harold Bloom alludes to Freud's ideas on narcissism, using them to critique the typological interpretation of Rachel and Beatrice.
Harold Bloom notes a parallel between Milton and Freud in their shared, yet evaded, intellectual debt to Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom cites Freud as a thinker who viewed religion as an illusion and whose work demonstrates an acceptance of the reality principle regarding death.
Harold Bloom invokes Freud's psychological concepts of Eros and Thanatos to interpret the forces at play in Faust.
Harold Bloom classifies Emerson as a 'wisdom writer' and groups him with other thinkers including Freud.
Harold Bloom references Sigmund Freud's potential theoretical disagreement with a formulation about the Sublime.
Harold Bloom references Freud's concept of 'the work of mourning' as an equivalent to Dickinson's poetic meditation.
Harold Bloom compares Dickinson's poetic negation to the intellectual projects of Nietzsche and Freud.
Harold Bloom references Freud's concept of 'reality testing' and his wisdom regarding accepting death, in contrast to Tolstoy and Hemingway.
Harold Bloom compares Ibsen's trolls to Freud's mythology of drives (Eros and Thanatos), suggesting a universal, partly trollish human nature.
Harold Bloom presents Freud as the codifier of psychoanalysis, which Shakespeare invented.
Harold Bloom summarizes Freud's psychoanalytic interpretation of Hamlet's character and actions.
Harold Bloom positions Freud as a foundational, myth-making figure comparable to major literary modernists.
Harold Bloom critiques Freud's interpretation of paternal relationships in King Lear.
Harold Bloom quotes and praises a line of Freud's writing as memorable wisdom.
Harold Bloom notes Freud's earlier observation about childlessness as central to Macbeth.
Harold Bloom references Freud's 1916 essay analyzing Lady Macbeth's character.
Harold Bloom agrees with Freud's assertion that Macbeth is fundamentally about childlessness.
Harold Bloom notes Freud's concession of interpretive limits regarding Macbeth, Hamlet, and King Lear.
Harold Bloom references Freud as a source of psychological concepts learned from Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom groups Freud with other authors as a canonical figure on the theme of sexual jealousy.
Harold Bloom cites a specific essay by Freud on sexual jealousy, positioning him as a rival to Proust on the topic.
Harold Bloom lists Freud among authors whose works constitute wisdom literature bordering on meditation.
Harold Bloom lists Freud among a group of modern canonical writers who share a lack of belief in God.
Harold Bloom references Freud's idea about religious impulses as a reductionist view that Kafka did not accept.
Harold Bloom references Freud's concept of the family romance in analyzing Borges' work.
Harold Bloom mentions Freud as another latecomer, like Schopenhauer, in representing the drive beyond the pleasure principle.
Harold Bloom references Freud's psychological theory to analyze the character dynamics in Endgame.
Harold Bloom cites Freud's conceptualization of anxiety to support his interpretation of the play's emotional tone.
Northrop Frye references Sade alongside other authors to argue that all such works are components of a liberal education, with decorum serving as the sole relevant moral standard.
Northrop Frye references Rimbaud's concept of 'illumination' as an example of the pure, transient vision in ironic thematic poetry.
Harold Bloom references the poet Rimbaud as a figure whose life is as enigmatic as his work.
Harold Bloom quotes a line from Rimbaud, presenting it alongside Novalis's as an example of despairing philosophical statements.
Harold Bloom cites Dostoevsky as a canonical figure whose preached ideas are morally problematic.
Harold Bloom cites Dostoevsky's use of Shakespearean villains as models for his own characters, drawing a parallel to the proposed link between Chaucer's Pardoner and Shakespeare's Iago and Edmund.
Harold Bloom references Dostoevsky's character Svidrigailov as a comparative example of preternatural intelligence used to violate trust, similar to the Pardoner and Iago.
Harold Bloom notes Wittgenstein's interest in Dostoevsky as an author.
Erich Auerbach cites Dostoevski, using the character Karamazov as an example of the modern realist capacity for creating tragic and psychologically complex figures.
Erich Auerbach references Dostoevski's character the Grand Inquisitor as a hypothetical example of a figure who could represent positive law in a conflict.
Erich Auerbach references Dostoevski as a prime example of a writer who depicts extreme psychological oscillations and direct expression of chaotic instinctive depths.
Erich Auerbach cites Dostoevski as a writer whose work reflects the dramatic and confused process of Russia's encounter with modern European civilization.
Northrop Frye references Spengler's ideas to illustrate a common poetic and critical tendency to view civilization through a cyclical, organic lens.
Northrop Frye identifies Spengler as a philosophical historian who explicitly postulates a quasi-organic rhythm of cultural aging.
Northrop Frye uses Shakespeare as an example to distinguish between a statement of fact and a generally accepted value-judgement in criticism.
Northrop Frye references Shakespeare as an exemplar of high mimetic decorum in drama, where the poet's personality is effaced.
Northrop Frye mentions Shakespeare alongside Jonson to illustrate how writers of the formal phase create works that transcend specific historical periods despite using historical material.

Northrop Frye uses Shakespeare as an example to illustrate that a poet's primary intention is centripetal, directed toward creating a coherent artistic work rather than conveying specific external meanings.
Northrop Frye references Shakespeare's plays 'King Lear' and 'Macbeth' as examples of intrinsic mystery in art, where greatness stems from revelation rather than concealment.
Northrop Frye references critical theories about Shakespeare's personal emotional state during a supposed 'tragic period' to challenge the idea that art produces real emotion in the creator.
Northrop Frye cites Shakespeare to illustrate that even great poets closely follow sources, arguing against the overvaluation of residual originality.
Northrop Frye references Shakespeare's forest comedies as part of the extended tradition of pastoral symbolism.
Northrop Frye references Shakespeare's character Miranda as an example of chastity associated with young women in the analogy of innocence.
Northrop Frye cites Shakespeare's works as containing examples of the usurping wicked uncle character type.
Northrop Frye references Shakespeare's late romances, Pericles and The Tempest, as exhibiting a tendency toward moral stratification of characters.
Northrop Frye quotes a character from Shakespeare to illustrate the limitations of invective and the need for impersonal moral standards in satire.
Northrop Frye references a Shakespearean example ('death’s dateless night') to illustrate a conventional figure of speech involving the fusion of concrete and abstract elements.
Richard Dawkins recalls a line from Shakespeare to humorously illustrate a point about lawyers and adversarial systems.
Harold Bloom references Shakespeare as the overwhelming example of canonical strangeness that becomes a given.
Harold Bloom asserts that Shakespeare's plays, more than Dante's work, are the true 'book and school of the ages'.
Harold Bloom references Shakespeare's political views, using the character Coriolanus as a point of comparison.
Harold Bloom mentions Shakespeare as a cornerstone of the Western Canon and educational tradition.
Harold Bloom references Shakespeare's plays 'Coriolanus', 'Hamlet', and 'King Lear' while discussing Harold Bloom's possible personal politics and anxieties.
Harold Bloom again identifies Shakespeare as a core canonical figure, exemplified by the introspective character Hamlet.
Harold Bloom notes Milton's personal identification with Shakespeare as a source of influence and legacy.
Harold Bloom discusses Shakespeare's life and prolific output as a playwright.
Harold Bloom references Shakespeare in the context of a historical era, citing Ortega and Madariaga's conclusion.
Harold Bloom states Shakespeare's influence persists in the modern Chaotic Age, specifically on Joyce and Beckett.
Harold Bloom credits Shakespeare with inventing a form of irony that underlies Freud's work.
Harold Bloom identifies Shakespeare as one of the few Western writers who possesses authentic universality.
Harold Bloom asserts that Shakespeare, alongside Cervantes's Don Quixote, centers the Canon for general readers.
Harold Bloom contrasts Dante's characters with those of Shakespeare, highlighting their development.
Harold Bloom describes Shakespeare as a central, anxiety-inducing influence on Milton's work and canonical standing.
Harold Bloom references Shakespeare as the creator of the characters Iago and Macbeth, contrasting his dramatic method with Milton's.
Harold Bloom discusses Johnson's critical analysis of Shakespeare's play 'Measure for Measure'.
Harold Bloom cites Curtius's view that Goethe is the culmination of a literary tradition that includes Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom discusses Shakespeare's influence on Goethe's 'Faust', noting Goethe's acknowledgment of Shakespeare's superiority.
Harold Bloom notes Goethe's artistic debt to Shakespeare regarding the dramatic use of apotheosis.
Harold Bloom describes Goethe's Faust as a sustained parody of Shakespeare's works.
Harold Bloom mentions Shakespeare as a heroic precursor who haunted Wordsworth.
Harold Bloom references Shakespeare's ideas about hope and despair in King Lear as an imperfect analogue to Wordsworth's theme.
Harold Bloom argues that Whitman's significance transcends gender, comparing him in this regard to Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom references Shakespeare as an underlying influence on Dickinson's poetic technique of substitution.
Harold Bloom cites Shakespeare as a source of surprising underground affiliations in Dickinson's work.
Harold Bloom references Shakespeare to describe a state of bleak exultation, comparing it to the emotional impact at the end of Hamlet.
Harold Bloom contrasts the inventiveness of Bleak House with the creative mode of Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom places Tolstoy in the canonical company of Shakespeare, among others.
Harold Bloom notes that Tolstoy's treatise 'What Is Art?' denounced Shakespeare, among others.
Harold Bloom describes Tolstoy's protagonist as a Shakespearean version of Tolstoy himself, referencing Shakespeare's dramatic influence.
Harold Bloom claims Tolstoy learned narrative techniques from Shakespeare, specifically the art of scene juxtaposition.
Harold Bloom notes Tolstoy's criticism of Shakespeare regarding character language, referencing Shakespeare's dramatic style.
Harold Bloom mentions Tolstoy's mixed reactions to Shakespeare's characters Falstaff and King Lear.
Harold Bloom suggests Tolstoy's character Anna Karenina contains Shakespearean elements, which Tolstoy resented.
Harold Bloom asserts Tolstoy harbored both hatred and fear towards Shakespeare as a literary figure.
Harold Bloom states that in 'Hadji Murad', Tolstoy achieves a level of artistry that rivals Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom claims Tolstoy absorbed Shakespeare's technique of vividly animating even minor characters.
Harold Bloom compares the extensive character list in 'Hadji Murad' to that of a major Shakespearean play.
Harold Bloom compares the depth of understanding of Hadji Murad to that of Shakespeare's warrior characters like Othello and Antony.
Harold Bloom notes that Tolstoy, like Shakespeare, adopts a voice distinct from his own to portray his protagonist.
Harold Bloom invokes Shakespeare as a benchmark for tragic protagonists.
Harold Bloom discusses Wittgenstein's and Tolstoy's troubled relationship with Shakespeare's works.
Harold Bloom compares Tolstoy's character Hadji Murad to Shakespeare's Antony, noting Tolstoy's gift for representing power struggles akin to Shakespeare's.
Harold Bloom compares Tolstoy's character portrayal to Shakespeare's methods.
Harold Bloom argues that Ibsen's character Hedda Gabler is derived from Shakespeare's villains Iago and Edmund.
Harold Bloom references Shakespeare's characters Iago and Edmund as precursors to Hedda Gabler, dismissing simplistic moral judgments of them as 'wicked fellows'.
Harold Bloom speculates that Ibsen viewed Shakespeare's hero-villains like Macbeth as trolls, while noting this interpretation isn't inherently Shakespearean.
Harold Bloom draws a parallel between the rancid playfulness in Shakespeare's Iago, Edmund, and Falstaff and the trollishness in Ibsen's Hedda Gabler.
Harold Bloom mentions Shakespeare as an author who, like Ibsen, does not focus on the theme of the Fall of Man.
Harold Bloom argues that Freud's psychological theories are fundamentally derived from his reading of Shakespeare's plays.
Harold Bloom states that Freud recognized Shakespeare as the greatest writer.
Harold Bloom credits Shakespeare as the inventor of psychoanalysis, positioning him as a precursor to Freud.
Harold Bloom argues that Joyce, despite his ambition, is not the fulfillment of a tradition for which Shakespeare was the forerunner.
Harold Bloom quotes Joyce stating a preference for Shakespeare over Dante due to the former's greater richness of characters.
Harold Bloom discusses Joyce's engagement with Shakespeare's works, particularly 'Macbeth', as a source of allusion and thematic inspiration in 'Finnegans Wake'.
Harold Bloom notes the structural use of Shakespeare's plays, specifically 'Macbeth' and 'King Lear', as framing allusions in Joyce's 'Finnegans Wake'.
Harold Bloom quotes directly from Shakespeare's 'Macbeth' to illustrate a textual echo in Joyce's 'Finnegans Wake'.
Harold Bloom references Hodgart's analysis showing how Joyce disperses soliloquies from Shakespeare's 'Macbeth' and 'Hamlet' throughout 'Finnegans Wake'.
Harold Bloom references Shakespeare as an example in Borges' pantheistic view of authors.
Harold Bloom notes Borges's ambiguous portrayal of Shakespeare, comparing him to family warriors and discussing his spiritual attribute of vagueness.
Harold Bloom cites Shakespeare's characters Falstaff and Macbeth as exemplars of the 'will to live'.
Harold Bloom states Shakespeare's Hamlet haunted Beckett and pervades his play 'Endgame'.
Harold Bloom states Beckett's work presupposes a reader familiar with canonical authors including Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom predicts Beckett's dramatic work will have the longevity of canonical playwrights like Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom states that 'Endgame' is constructed from a paradigm drawing on specific plays by Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom identifies Shakespeare's fools, particularly Feste, as influences behind Beckett's characters.
Harold Bloom asserts that 'Endgame' contains revisions or reworkings of specific plays by Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom positions Shakespeare's work as foundational scripture in contrast to Beckett's commentary.
Erich Auerbach references Shakespeare as an example of a writer whose work is stirred by the uncertainty of human existence or the power of destiny, contrasting this with Cervantes's attitude.
Erich Auerbach cites Shakespeare as a benchmark for literary works that elicit deep reader sympathy and participation, contrasting him with memoirists like Retz.
Erich Auerbach notes that the technique of mixing styles in German literature was adopted under the influence of Shakespeare's work.
Erich Auerbach references Shakespeare as a key figure in the romantic debate advocating for a mixture of literary styles, contrasted with Racine.
Erich Auerbach notes that Flaubert, despite his own realist aims, viewed these authors through a romanticist lens, attracted by great subjects and free imagination.
Northrop Frye mentions Bunyan as an example of a writer who uses continuous allegory, comparing his works to musical compositions in literature.

Northrop Frye lists Bunyan among other writers as examples of works that constitute a liberal education, emphasizing that moral judgment in art should be based on decorum rather than external standards.
Northrop Frye references Aristotle's methodological assumption about the primary step in criticism.

Northrop Frye links a literary pole to Aristotle's concept of mythos, referencing his terminology.
Northrop Frye mentions Aristotle's categorization of poetic aspects, setting up a framework for further discussion.

Northrop Frye references Aristotle as an authority on the definition of a poem.

Northrop Frye references Aristotle's understanding of tragedy as a genre to illustrate the concept of a poem belonging to a class of similar forms.
Northrop Frye references Aristotle as an early and influential critic whose views on metaphor represent a critical consensus.

Northrop Frye references Aristotle's concept of 'spoudaios' as a quality in art, linking it to the convergence of religion and poetry within a moral framework.
Northrop Frye acknowledges Aristotle's foundational contribution to the theory of tragedy, noting that it provides a more established framework compared to other literary forms.
Northrop Frye references Aristotle's ideas on tragedy, specifically the importance of plot-structure, without naming a specific book.
Northrop Frye references Aristotle's ethical concept of proairesis in relation to tragic hamartia, noting Aristotle's tendency to view tragedy as morally intelligible.
Northrop Frye references the portrayal of Aristotle in Lyly's play as an example of philosophers being satirized as dull.
Northrop Frye cites Aristotle's concept of ethos as a central component of the poetic symbol, situated between mythos and dianoia.
Northrop Frye notes Aristotle's enumeration of six elements of poetry, focusing on three of them.
Northrop Frye references Aristotle's observation in the Poetics that the subject of lexis is more appropriately part of rhetoric.
Northrop Frye references Aristotle's concept of 'melos' to define a technical term in literary criticism.

Northrop Frye mentions Aristotle as one of the classical critics who grappled with the paradoxical origins of tragedy in the satyr-play.
Northrop Frye references Aristotelian logic as a stock example where the containing forms of conceptual thought, specifically subject and predicate, have a grammatical origin.
Northrop Frye uses Aristotle's concept of 'nature' as an example of a key connotative term whose full understanding could unlock a philosopher's entire system.

Northrop Frye cites Aristotle as a philosopher whose work on poetics can be used independently of his broader philosophical system.
Northrop Frye mentions Aristotle's disapproval of a certain processional structure in literature.
Northrop Frye references Aristotle's concept of melopoiia as the source for the term 'melos'.

Harold Bloom uses Aristotle's term 'dianoia' to analyze the thought content in Goethe's work.

Edward Gibbon mentions that Caracalla persecuted the disciples of Aristotle, referencing the philosopher's intellectual school.
Edward Gibbon references Aristotle as a philosopher whose ideas, along with Plato's, were the subject of futile reconciliation attempts by the new Platonists.

Thomas S. Kuhn references Aristotle as a source of theoretical ideas in the context of competing schools in physical optics before Newton.
Thomas S. Kuhn references Aristotle's work as an example of a paradigm whose initial success was a promise based on selected examples, later elaborated through normal science.
Thomas S. Kuhn references Aristotle's proofs regarding the earth's stability as an earlier subject of criticism analogous to the critique of Newton.
Thomas S. Kuhn mentions Aristotelian explanations as being rejected by the new science of the seventeenth century.
Thomas S. Kuhn references Aristotelian beliefs about motion and natural rest, attributing them to Aristotle's influence.
Thomas S. Kuhn references Aristotle as a historical figure whose paradigm influenced the perception and measurement of falling bodies, contrasting it with Galileo's approach.

Northrop Frye cites Milton's terminology regarding the 'matter' of a song as an example of precise literary language from a past era.

Northrop Frye references Milton's practice of borrowing from the Bible to challenge low mimetic prejudices about creation and originality.
Northrop Frye references Milton's own work to note his description of the 'annual wound' associated with Adonis.
Northrop Frye cites Milton's depiction of the garden of Eden as belonging to the analogy of innocence rather than the apocalyptic structure.
Northrop Frye quotes Milton to support a point about satire's aim to target prominent vices in high places.
Northrop Frye describes Milton's prose as possessing musical qualities, akin to his verse.

Northrop Frye groups Milton with Homer and Virgil as representative of the typical epic structure in the high mimetic mode.

Harold Bloom references Milton as a poet who made pragmatic compromises, alluding to his epic 'Paradise Lost'.

Harold Bloom mentions Milton as an example of a writer who, like others, could not match Tolstoy's solipsism.

Our original-text editions include the following visual enhancements to foster a deeper understanding of the work: Word Clouds at the start of each chapter highlight important words. Co-occurrence graphs depict character-to-character interactions as well character to place interactions. Sentiment indexes identify positive and....
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Plato's dialogue 'Phaedrus' as a work that treats poetry as myth.

book:26188710.description: PLATO (428/427 bc - 348/347 bc), was a Classical Greek philosopher, mathematician, writer of philosophical dialogues, and founder of the Academy in Athens, the first institution of higher learning in the western world.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Plato's 'Cratylus' for its introduction of ironic literary techniques.

book:18242296.description: The Republic, written in 380BC by the great philosopher and thinker Plato, is the longest and greatest of his works. Originally titled as politeria, meaning 'City-State governance' in Greek, it actually proposes a Just society ruled by a philosopher- the King and the guardian. Written in the form of dialogues between his teacher Socrates and various Athenians, it discusses the meaning of Justice and its nature, and goes on to examine whether or not the Just society. Along the way are the discussions on immo...
commentaries: Erich Auerbach states that his investigation began with Plato's philosophical discussion of mimesis in the Republic.
Northrop Frye references the conclusion of Plato's 'Republic' as a polemic against a specific mode of poetry.
Northrop Frye cites Plato's Republic as an example of the body metaphor applied to political organization.
Northrop Frye references Plato's Republic as an example of a dialogue where a contest between characters leads into a deeper contemplation of a just state.

book:8340956.description:
(The) Apology (of Socrates) is Plato's version of the speech given by Socrates as he defends himself against the charges of being a man "who corrupted the young, did not believe in the gods, and created new deities". "Apology" here has its earlier meaning (now usually expressed by the word "apologia") of speaking in defense of a cause or of one's beliefs or actions.
This book was converted from its physical edition to the digital format by a community of volunteers. You may find it for free on the web. Purc...
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Plato's work as a masterpiece of tragic irony, contrasting it with the comic conclusion of Aristophanes' play.

book:web_7fe4ff44.description: A periodical publication by Samuel Taylor Coleridge, later collected into a single volume, containing essays on philosophy, politics, and literature. The 'Essay on Method' appears in the 1818 edition.
commentaries: Northrop Frye references an essay by Coleridge from this work, while noting his interpretation may not be strictly correct.

book:web_436ef14a.description: A collection of Coleridge's critical writings edited by Thomas Middleton Raysor, published by Harvard University Press in 1936.
commentaries: Northrop Frye directs the reader to Coleridge's collected criticism, noting an expansion of Coleridge's idea to clarify a critical principle.

book:484422.description: Wuthering Heightsis a wild, passionate story of the intense and almost demonic love between Catherine Earnshaw and Heathcliff, a foundling adopted by Catherine's father. After Mr. Earnshaw's death, Heathcliff is bullied and humiliated by Catherine's brother Hindley and wrongly believing that his love for Catherine is not reciprocated, leaves Wuthering Heights, only to return years later as a wealthy and polished man. He proceeds to exact a terrible revenge for his former miseries. The action of the story is...
commentaries: Northrop Frye references Brontë's 'Wuthering Heights' as employing a male version of the two-heroine convention.

book:7542784.description: Honore Balzac, dit Honore de Balzac (1799-1850) est un romancier, critique litteraire, essayiste, journaliste et ecrivain francais. Il est considere comme l'un des plus grands ecrivains francais dans le domaine du roman realiste, du roman philosophique et du roman fantastique par Gerard Gengembre, G. Vannier, le philosophe Alain, et Albert Beguin. Charles Baudelaire voyait en lui un visionnaire. Balzac est cependant difficile a classer dans l'une ou l'autre categorie, son oeuvre couvrant un champ si vaste q...
commentaries: Erich Auerbach cites this novel as a source of realistic observation on the exhausting life of Parisians during the early bourgeois monarchy.

book:914758.description:
<>, s'exclame Balzac au moment ou il ecrit Le Pere Goriot. Il venait d'imaginer La Comedie humaine, ce cycle romanesque dans lequel les memes personnages reapparaissent d'un roman a l'autre. Il venait de creer un monde, le monde balzacien.
Les plus beaux romans, dit Andre Maurois, sont des romans d'apprentissage. Les illusions de la jeunesse s'y heurtent au monde feroce et pourtant plein de delices. L'amour devient coquetterie, la vertu s'achete, l'argent ruine tout. Seule la passion balzacienne, ici l'amou...
commentaries: Erich Auerbach uses Balzac's novel 'Le Père Goriot' as a specific example to illustrate Balzac's realistic method of character and milieu description.

book:985716.description: The love of money and a passionate pursuit of it are seen as a driving force in post-Revolutionary France, and are studied in detail in the character of Grandet.
commentaries: Erich Auerbach cites Balzac's novel as an example of a work that consciously connects individual fortunes to broader historical events.
Erich Auerbach cites Balzac's novel as a contrasting example of detailed, historically interwoven economic realism, in opposition to Molière's ahistorical treatment.

book:17678810.description:
Gulzar, one of India' finest film-makers and lyricists, has always been a poet at heart. His oeuvre is steeped in a poetic sensibility, marked by a lyricism rare in the world of Hindi cinema. Born in 1934, Gulzar's journey as a poet began with the Progressive Writers' Movement. Today, he is regarded as one of India's foremost Urdu Poets, unparalleled in his exploration of human relationships and the insights and sensitivity with which he addresses the many facets of daily life.
Whether evoking an abiding no...
commentaries: Northrop Frye references this specific edition for a poem ('Camellia Sabina'), noting textual variations in later editions.
Northrop Frye references Rasselas as an example of a 'prison-Paradise or unborn world' from which characters seek escape.
Harold Bloom commends Johnson's prose-romance Rasselas as a superb work.

book:web_a711a558.description: A pastoral play by Elizabethan dramatist George Peele, written as court entertainment celebrating Queen Elizabeth I. It features mythological characters and concludes with Paris presenting the golden apple to Elizabeth.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Peele's play 'Arraignment of Paris' as an example of a secular drama with parallels to religious mystery plays.

book:2541248.description: Volpone tells of a magnifico of Venice with no wife or children to whom to leave his fortune. The prospect of such wealth invites to his house an assortment of greedy hopefuls, ready to prostitute any ideals in the pursuit of money. Volpone's parasite, Mosca, assists him in milking these pretenders as they deserve. When Volpone and Mosca practice their schemes on innocent victims, however, the play turns in a more unpredictable direction and ends in a series of surprises. Subplot figures enrich the narrativ...
commentaries: Harold Bloom references characters from Jonson's plays, Volpone and The Alchemist, to illustrate unchanging character types.

book:784860.description: A new critical edition of a literary masterpieceA farsighted Victorian, William Morris was a pioneering socialist, book designer and decorative artist, founder of the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings, and author of intense short lyrics, long poetic narratives, and utopian-socialist prose romances. This annotated critical edition is the first attempt to make Morris's 42,000 word verse sequence accessible to a modern audience. The edition's scholarly apparatus also records the location of extan...
commentaries: Northrop Frye describes The Earthly Paradise as a very pure example of the contemplative phase where old men interchange myths in a dreamlike land.

book:716523.description: This book was converted from its physical edition to the digital format by a community of volunteers. You may find it for free on the web. Purchase of the Kindle edition includes wireless delivery.
commentaries: Northrop Frye references The Sundering Flood as an example where a dividing river symbolizes a sexual barrier.

book:1410532.description:
Acknowledged by T. S. Eliot as one of the chief sources for his great poem "The Waste Land," Jessie L. Weston's From Ritual to Romanceremains a landmark of anthropological and mythological scholarship. In this book she explores the origins of the Grail legend, arguing that it dates back to a primitive vegetation cult and only later was shaped by Celtic and Christian lore.
To prove her thesis, Weston unites folkloric and Christian elements by using printed texts to prove the parallels existing between each a...
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites this book as the source for a claim ('we are told') in the narrative.

book:1990743.description: The only unabridged prose translation of Ariosto's Orlando Furioso- a witty parody of the chivalric legends of Charlemagne and the Saracen invasion of France - this version faithfully recaptures the entire narrative and the subtle meanings behind it.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Orlando Furioso as an example of a Renaissance narrative where the primary interest is storytelling, though it can be interpreted thematically.
Harold Bloom identifies Ariosto's 'Orlando Furioso' as the great prototype for Don Quixote's madness, specifically citing the character Orlando's erotic madness.

book:1853180.description:
More successful in its day than The Way of the World, which is now
accounted Congreve's best play, Love for Love (1695) is a comical farce manifesting the verbal polish and the theatrical wit that audiences so enjoy in Congreve. Valentine, Sir Sampson's dissolute eldest son, finds himself at a standstill; the only way out of his financial difficulties is to give in to his father's pressure to renounce his right of inheritance. While this suggestion immediately increases the chances of his bluff younger brot...
commentaries: Northrop Frye analyzes Love for Love to highlight Oedipal themes and comic infidelity in Restoration comedy.

book:7008439.description: William Congreve (1670-1729) was an English playwright and poet. He wrote some of the most popular English plays of the Restoration period of the late 17th century. By the age of thirty, he had written four comedies, including Love for Love (premiered 1695) and The Way of the World (premiered 1700), and one tragedy, The Mourning Bride (1697). After writing five plays from his first in 1693 until 1700, he produced no more as public tastes turned against the sort of highbrow sexual comedy of manners in which....
commentaries: Harold Bloom notes Johnson's lapse in praising a passage from Congreve's Mourning Bride above Shakespeare.

book:12414975.description: Breaking from Freud by allowing for nonsexual psychic forces driving the libido, Carl Jung made a more lasting name for himself than did his mentor. Psychology of the Unconsciousis a prodigious leap away from Freud's dictatorial constraints, exploring the mythic aspects of our interior lives in exquisite detail. While he sometimes sacrifices readability for erudition, this is no failing for the interested student, who strives to follow Jung as he moves from Norse mythology to Shakespeare to Sanskrit etymolo...
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites this work, noting it is soon to be retranslated, in a discussion of the hero archetype.

book:2491573.description:
Verso la fine degli anni venti Jung scopre singolari affinita tra antichi simboli cinesi e i sogni dei suoi pazienti: comincia cosi a studiare i testi degli alchimisti. Dopo quindici anni di lavoro pubblica questo volume, che rimane fra i suoi testi piu affascinanti. La tradizione alchimistica e la pratica analitica hanno in comune il tentativo di creare una realta nuova e superiore: da una parte l'oro, la pietra filosofale, dall'altra la "presa di coscienza" della psicologia moderna.
L'alchimia e espressio...
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites this book as a source on alchemical symbolism.

book:11721378.description: When Carl Gustav Jung and Karl Kerenyi got together to collaborate on this book, their aim was to elevate the study of mythology to a science. Kerenyi wrote on two of the most ubiquitous myths, the "Divine Child" & "The Maiden", supporting the core "stories" with both an introduction & a conclusion. Jung then provided a psychological analysis of both myths. He defined myth as a story about heroes interacting with the gods. Having long studied dreams & the unconscious, Jung identified certain dream patterns....
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites this collaborative work as further reading on mythological science.

book:1210925.description: The essays in "Criticism" include fifteen "Contemporary Reviews" that locate the problems of the novel pursued by later critics in a more detailed and sophisticated fashion "Modern Essays in Criticism" represent the perspec-tives of Irving Howe, Roy R. Male, A. N. Kaul, Leo B. Levy, Hans-Joachim Lang, Philip Rahv, Allan B. Lefcowitz, Barbara F. Lefcowitz, Nina Baym, Hyatt H. Waggoner, Frederick C. Crews, Kelley Griffith, Jr., Louis Auchincloss, James H. Justus, and Kent Bales.
commentaries: Northrop Frye references The Blithedale Romance as an example of a contemplative, idyllic view of experience from above.

book:12399131.description: In a sleepy little New England village stands a dark, weather-beaten, many-gabled house. This brooding mansion is haunted by a centuries-old curse that casts the shadow of ancestral sin upon the last four members of the distinctive Pyncheon family of Salem. The greed and haughty pride of the Pyncheon family through the generations is mirrored in the gloomy decay of their seven-gabled mansion, where the family's enfeebled and impoverished relations now live. Mysterious deaths threaten the living. Musty docum...
commentaries: Northrop Frye references Hawthorne's own preface to illustrate the distinction between romance and novel forms.

book:639803.description: The pointed and furry ears, therefore, are the sole indications of his wild, forest nature. Only a sculptor of the finest imagination, the most delicate taste, the sweetest feeling, and the rarest artistic skill -- in a word, a sculptor and a poet too -- could have first dreamed of a Faun in this guise, and then have succeeded in imprisoning the sportive and frisky thing in marble. Neither man nor animal, and yet no monster, but a being in whom both races meet on friendly ground. The idea grows coarse as we...
commentaries: Northrop Frye uses Hawthorne's novel as an example of romance where a character is strongly associated with a statue, illustrating how close romance can come to myth through significant association rather than direct identity.
Northrop Frye cites Hawthorne's 'The Marble Faun' as an example of a nineteenth-century novel using the convention of two heroines, one dark and one light.

book:9491612.description: "The Alcestis would hardly confirm its author's right to be acclaimed 'the most tragic of the poets.' It is doubtful whether one can call it a tragedy at all. Yet it remains one of the most characteristic and delightful of Euripidean dramas, as well as, by modern standards, the most easily actable. And I notice that many judges who display nothing but a fierce satisfaction in sending other plays of that author to the block or the treadmill, show a certain human weakness in sentencing the gentle daughter of....
commentaries: Northrop Frye analyzes Euripides' Alcestis as a tragedy of the first phase, focusing on the calumniated woman figure.

book:6021378.description:
In Troezen, a NE Peloponnese coastal polis, King Theseus of Athens, is serving a year's voluntary exile after having murdered a local king & his sons. His illegitimate son Hippolytus, whose mother is the Amazon Hippolyta, has been trained here since childhood by the king of Troezen, Pittheus.
At the play's opening Aphrodite explains that Hippolytus has sworn chastity, refusing reverence. He honors the virgin huntress, Artemis. This has led her to initiate a vengeful plan. When Hippolytus went to Athens two....
commentaries: Northrop Frye references the tragedy of Hippolytus as an example of youthful inexperience leading to disaster.

book:1152993.description: One of Euripides' late plays, Ion tells the story of Kreousa, queen of Athens, and her son by the god Apollo. Apollo raped Kreousa; she secretly abandoned their child, assuming thereafter that the god had allowed him to die. Ion, however, is saved to become a ward of Apollo's temple at Delphi. In the play, Kreousa and her husband Xouthos go to Delphi to seek a remedy for their childlessness; Apollo, speaking through his oracle, gives Ion to Xouthos as a son, enraging the apparently still childless Kreousa.....
commentaries: Northrop Frye references Euripides' play 'Ion' as part of the historical development of birth-mystery plot formulas.

book:24658.description:
'What was the beginning, or how did things start? What was there before?'
The Prose Eddais the most renowned of all works of Scandinavian literature and our most extensive source for Norse mythology. Written in Iceland a century after the close of the Viking Age, it tells ancient stories of the Norse creation epic and recounts the battles that follow as gods, giants, dwarves and elves struggle for survival. It also preserves the oral memory of heroes, warrior kings and queens. In clear prose interspersed wi...
commentaries: Northrop Frye classifies the Prose Edda as a sacred book belonging to the same quintessential form as the Bible, and notes its influence on Finnegans Wake.

book:web_e6dcbfc8.description: A scholarly work examining the origins and development of ancient Greek comedy, particularly its ritual and mythological foundations.
commentaries: Northrop Frye references Cornford's book as the source for a suggestion regarding the structure of Old Comedy.

book:15828826.description: Sens and Sensibility's two heroines - so utterly unlike each other - undergo the most violent passions when they are separated from the men they love. What differentiates them, and gives this extraordinary book its complexity and brilliance is the way each expresses her suffering. Marianne - young, impetuous, ardent - falls into paroxysms of grief when she is rejected by the dashing John Willoughby; while her sister, Elinor - wiser, more sensible, more self-controlled - masks her despair when it appears tha...
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Austen's novel as an example of a work named for its theme, while noting Austen's interest in storytelling.

book:2534657.description: In Northanger Abbey, a young woman's penchant for sensational Gothic novels leads to misunderstandings in the matters of the heart. Austen's first, this is considered by many to be among her most charming novels.
commentaries: Northrop Frye lists this novel as an example of a work that parodies romance conventions.

book:1555826.description: In this historic romance, young Elizabeth Bennet strives for love, independence and honesty in the vapid high society of 19th century England.
commentaries: Northrop Frye uses Austen's novel as an example to discuss how a shift in focus could undermine humor and evoke a sense of nightmare in comedy.
Northrop Frye contrasts Austen's Pride and Prejudice with Hyperion as examples of the division between fictional and thematic works in the low mimetic mode.
Harold Bloom quotes Woolf speculating about Austen's circumstances affecting her writing.

book:web_9f8f8c04.description: One of the Canterbury Tales, a collection of stories written in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer in the late 14th century. The Franklin's Tale explores themes of marriage, honor, and generosity.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites The Franklin's Tale as an example of mature innocent wisdom in a contemplative, erotic world.

book:2339726.description: On a spring day in April--sometime in the waning years of the 14th century--29 travelers set out for Canterbury on a pilgrimage to the shrine of Saint Thomas Beckett. Among them is a knight, a monk, a prioress, a plowman, a miller, a merchant, a clerk, and an oft-widowed wife from Bath. Travel is arduous and wearing; to maintain their spirits, this band of pilgrims entertains each other with a series of tall tales that span the spectrum of literary genres. Five hundred years later, people are still reading....
commentaries: Harold Bloom identifies Chaucer as Shakespeare's truest precursor, specifically referencing his work 'Canterbury Tales' as the source of the literary debt for the character Falstaff.
Harold Bloom lists this work as one of the few more essential to the Western Canon than Paradise Lost.

book:1131671.description: Ranking #401,312 on Amazon.com's best seller list, Fowler's idiosyncracic masterpiece dedicates itself to discussing (sometimes pedantically, sometimes whimsically, always insightfully) how and why we use and misuse a few thousand English words, one of which is "one." Fowler's discussion of "one" goes on for 3+ pages and includes a section on what he calls the "false first-person one," which is using one instead of/in place of I. In 1944, Fowler noted its presence only in journalism, where "it enables the s...
commentaries: Northrop Frye mentions consulting a specific article in Fowler's reference work to clarify his terminology.

book:18211374.description: Laurence Sterne's great masterpiece of bawdy humour and rich satire defies any attempt to categorize it. Part novel, part digression, its gloriously disordered narrative interweaves the birth and life of the unfortunate "hero" Tristram Shandy, the eccentric philosophy of his father Walter, the amours and military obsessions of Uncle Toby, and a host of other characters, including Dr. Slop, Corporal Trim and the parson Yorick. A joyful celebration of the endless possibilities of the art of fiction, Tristram....
commentaries: Harold Bloom mentions Johnson's erroneous judgment that Sterne's Tristram Shandy would not endure.

book:18963915.description: Erasmus of Rotterdam (c. 1466-1536) is one of the greatest figures of the Renaissance humanist movement, which abandoned medieval pieties in favour of a rich new vision of the individual's potential. Praise of Folly, written to amuse his friend Sir Thomas More, is Erasmus's best-known work. Its dazzling mixture of fantasy and satire is narrated by a personification of Folly, dressed as a jester, who celebrates youth, pleasure, drunkenness and sexual desire, and goes on to lambast human pretensions, foibles....
commentaries: Northrop Frye references Erasmus's book as part of the encyclopaedic satire tradition, illustrating its connection to comic phases.

book:4225755.description: This is one of seven volumes that will contain the more than 4000 adages that Erasmus gathered and commented on, sometimes in a few lines and sometimes in full-scale essays. The notes identify the classical sources and indicate how Erasmus' reading and thinking developed over the quarter-century spanned by the eight revisions of the original work. Many of the proverbs cited by Erasmus are still in our common stock of speech.
commentaries: Erich Auerbach suggests Erasmus's Adagia as a possible direct source for Rabelais's use of the Silenus comparison.
Northrop Frye cites this book for an analysis of thematic repetition in Forster's work.
Northrop Frye cites the novel as an example of tragic irony where crime is deeply tied to character, contrasting it with the manipulated suspicion in detective stories.
Harold Bloom compares Edmund's nihilistic qualities to characters in Dostoevsky's novel.

book:20520939.description: Pyotr and Stavrogin are the leaders of a Russian revolutionary cell. Their aim is to overthrow the Tsar, destroy society, and seize power for themselves. Together they train terrorists who are willing to lay down their lives to accomplish their goals. But when the group is threatened with exposure, will their recruits be willing to kill one of their own to cover their tracks? Savage and powerful yet lively and often comic, Demons was inspired by a real-life political murder and is a scathing and eerily pres...
commentaries: Harold Bloom cites Stavrogin as another Dostoevskian nihilist comparable to Edmund.
Erich Auerbach cites Dostoevski's novels as examples of the non-specific, homogeneous settings characteristic of Russian literature.

book:11057575.description:
The final masterpiece from the celebrated author of "Crime and Punishment" and "The Idiot."..
This extraordinary novel, Dostoyevsky s last and greatest work, tells the dramatic story of four brothers Dmitri, pleasure-seeking, impatient, unruly . . . Ivan, brilliant and morose . . . Alyosha, gentle, loving, honest . . . and the illegitimate Smerdyakov, sly, silent, cruel. Driven by intense passion, they become involved in the brutal murder of their own father, one of the most loathsome characters in all lite...
commentaries: Erich Auerbach again references Dostoevski's novel to illustrate the uniformity of setting in Russian realism.
Erich Auerbach uses characters and settings from Dostoevski's novels as examples to illustrate the patriarchal nature of the Russian merchant class.
Northrop Frye references Kierkegaard's book to illustrate the concept of 'repetition' as a creative and redemptive act, contrasting it with Platonic recollection.

book:9004295.description: In Timore e tremore Kierkegaard tenta di rispondere all'angoscioso dilemma della rinuncia, il sacrificio richiesto dalla ragione: la dimensione del silenzio e dell'assurdo pieno di solitudine e di sofferenza della fede, che <>. Raccontando la storia di Abramo e la paradossalita del sacrificio del figlio Isacco che gli viene chiesto da Dio, Kierkegaard mostra la radicalita dell'atteggiamento religioso. Una rassegnazione infinita e un credere nell'assurdo che inducono l'autore a porre il problema del rapporto...
commentaries: Harold Bloom suggests Kafka's interpretation of Abraham was a critical response to Kierkegaard's work 'Fear and Trembling'.

book:web_8c2a3697.description: A collection of Cicero's letters to various friends and acquaintances, compiled after his death. The work is a primary source for the history of the late Roman Republic.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon quotes a letter from Cicero to illustrate the peril of political exiles under a single ruler.

book:18086086.description: Cicero's On the Commonwealth and On the Laws are his most important works of political philosophy. The present volume offers a scholarly reconstruction of the fragments of On the Commonwealth and a masterly translation of both dialogues. The texts are supported by a helpful, concise introduction, notes and other aids. Students in politics, philosophy, ancient history, law and classics will gain a new understanding of this seminal thinker thanks to Professor Zetzel's volume.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Cicero's work 'de Legibus' to provide a definition for the consular power.
Edward Gibbon references Cicero's work 'de Legibus' in a footnote concerning the actions of ancient kings.

book:551367.description: Cicero (Marcus Tullius, 10643 BCE), Roman lawyer, orator, politician and philosopher, of whom we know more than of any other Roman, lived through the stirring era which saw the rise, dictatorship, and death of Julius Caesar in a tottering republic. In his political speeches especially and in his correspondence we see the excitement, tension and intrigue of politics and the part he played in the turmoil of the time. Of about 106 speeches, delivered before the Roman people or the Senate if they were political...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Cicero's Tusculan Disputations as a source, though the specific point of citation is not detailed in the excerpt.

book:27616581.description: "Orator" from Marco Tullius Cicero. Cicero was a Roman philosopher, politician, lawyer, orator, political theorist, consul and constitutionalist (106-43 BC).
commentaries: Erich Auerbach critiques the translation of specific stylistic terms from Cicero's work.

book:web_347676c9.description: A short rhetorical treatise by Cicero, written around 52 BCE, which serves as a preface to his translations of speeches by Aeschines and Demosthenes. It discusses the ideal qualities of orators and the challenges of translation.
commentaries: Erich Auerbach mentions another of Cicero's works as being cited by Curtius.
Northrop Frye references The Sacred Fount as Henry James's exploration of a quixotic hero who constructs an illusory society.

book:web_df9230cd.description: An unfinished novel by Henry James, published posthumously in 1917. It explores themes of time travel and historical consciousness, following an American who inherits an English house and finds himself transported to the early 19th century.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites this novel as an example where the labyrinthine underworld theme is used in a sophisticated story, with the hero being released from a period of past time.

book:7105277.description: This groundbreaking English version by Robert Fagles is the most important recent translation of Homer's great epic poem. The verse translation has been hailed by scholars as the new standard, providing an Iliad that delights modern sensibility and aesthetic without sacrificing the grandeur and particular genius of Homer's own style and language. The Iliad is one of the two great epics of Homer, and is typically described as one of the greatest war stories of all time, but to say the Iliad is a war story do...
commentaries: Northrop Frye references Homer's Iliad to illustrate the concept of a divine double perspective in classical mythology.
Northrop Frye references the Iliad as an example where a central female figure polarizes the tragic conflict.
Northrop Frye lists the Iliad as an example of an epic, using it to define the customary use of the term 'epic'.
Northrop Frye analyzes the cyclical structure of the total action in Homer's 'Iliad'.
Northrop Frye states that the sense of stability that makes tragedy possible is present in the 'Iliad'.
Northrop Frye credits the 'Iliad' with introducing an objective, disinterested vision that grants poetry lasting authority.
Harold Bloom references Homer's epic as the original work whose sentiments and descriptions Pope adapted in his translation.
Harold Bloom mentions that a fictional manuscript in Borges's story was found in a specific edition of Pope's translation of Homer's 'Iliad', citing the original author Homer.
Harold Bloom references Homer's 'The Iliad' as an example of a canonical work that teaches values contrary to modern democratic principles.

book:8214389.description: The Odyssey is, quite simply, the story of Odysseus, who wants to go home. But Poseidon, god of oceans, doesn't want him to make it back across the wine-dark sea to his wife, Penelope, son, Telemachus, and their high-roofed home at Ithaca. The story is told in easy-going, beautiful poetry; the characters speak naturally, the action happens briskly. Even the gods come across as real people, despite the divine powers they exercise constantly.
commentaries: Northrop Frye lists the Odyssey as an example of an epic, using it to define the customary use of the term 'epic'.
Northrop Frye analyzes the cyclical structure of the total action in Homer's 'Odyssey'.
Northrop Frye identifies Homer's 'Odyssey' as the foundational work for the epic tradition of return.
Erich Auerbach references Homer's Odyssey as the source for the detailed scene of Odysseus's homecoming and recognition by Euryclea.
Harold Bloom compares Tolstoy's 'Hadji Murad' to Homer's epic 'The Odyssey' in its strangeness.

book:5891.description: Mistaken identities, locked rooms, madness, and romance--these are a few of the ingredients the author (one of the most successful and popular Victorian writers) used to inspire "the 'creepy' effect, as of pounded ice dropped down the back," that, according to one of his friends, was Wilkie Collins's aim in writing The Woman in White. Popularly regarded as one of the author's finest works, and widely copied by other writers, this thriller was the prototype for a whole new genre of fiction: the "sensation no...
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites 'The Woman in White' as an example of a nineteenth-century novel using the convention of two heroines, one dark and one light.

book:web_991320c7.description: A scholarly work by Gertrude Rachel Levy examining the origins and structures of epic literature, analyzing mythical epics, quest-epics, and conflict-epics. Published by Faber and Faber.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites this book to support a classification of epic frameworks, noting a correspondence with his own categories.

book:10139547.description: The 18th century was a wealth of knowledge, exploration and rapidly growing technology and expanding record-keeping made possible by advances in the printing press. commentaries: Harold Bloom references this poem as an example of Pope's inventive genius, according to Johnson's analysis.

book:web_39e6c2a0.description: A collection of four moral essays in verse by Alexander Pope, also known as the 'Ethick Epistles' or 'Moral Essays', addressing topics like the characters of men and women, the use of riches, and the nature of happiness.
commentaries: Harold Bloom cites these epistles as works where Pope's imagination impresses forms of nature and life.

book:web_cd5a428e.description: A topographical poem by Alexander Pope celebrating the peace following the Treaty of Utrecht, blending pastoral description with political commentary.
commentaries: Harold Bloom references this poem as another demonstration of Pope's imaginative power in depicting nature.

book:5613536.description: This work has been selected by scholars as being culturally important, and is part of the knowledge base of civilization as we know it. Therefore, you will see the original copyright references, library stamps (as most of these works have been housed in our most important libraries around the world), and other notations in the work.This work is in the public domain in the United States of America, and....
commentaries: Harold Bloom describes Johnson's critical dismissal of this philosophical poem by Pope.
Harold Bloom notes Johnson's high regard for this work by Pope, considering it superior to the Essay on Man.

book:408862.description: Before Joseph Campbell became the world's most famous practitioner of comparative mythology, there was Sir James George Frazer. The Golden Boughwas originally published in two volumes in 1890, but Frazer became so enamored of his topic that over the next few decades he expanded the work sixfold, then in 1922 cut it all down to a single thick edition suitable for mass distribution. The thesis on the origins of magic and religion that it elaborates "will be long and laborious," Frazer warns readers, "but may....
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Frazer's work as a key text for understanding the ritual content of naive drama, noting its influence on literary criticism despite being an anthropological study.

book:web_3f6b5d00.description: Comic opera in two acts, with libretto by W. S. Gilbert and music by Arthur Sullivan. It premiered in London in 1885 and satirizes British institutions and bureaucracy through a fictional Japanese setting.
commentaries: Northrop Frye references the operetta as a clearer example of ritualistic sacrifice themes than found in Aristophanes, highlighting its explicit parody elements.

book:6012840.description: Don Quixotehas become so entranced by reading chivalric romances, that he determines to become a knight-errant himself. In the company of his faithful squire, Sancho Panza, his exploits blossom in all sorts of wonderful ways. While Quixote's fancy often leads him astray - he tilts at windmills, imagining them to be giants - Sancho acquires cunning and a certain sagacity. Sane madman and wise fool, they roam the world together, and together they have haunted readers' imaginations for nearly four hundred year...
commentaries: Northrop Frye mentions this book as establishing a tradition of parodying romance conventions within the novel form.

book:9404675.description: This anthology contains English translations of five plays by two of the best practitioners of Roman comedy, Plautus and Terence. The plays, Menaechmi, Rudens, Truculentus, Adelphoe, and Eunuchus, provide an introduction to the world of Roman comedy. As with all Focus translations, the emphasis is on a handsomely produced, inexpensive, readable edition that is close to the original, with an extensive introduction, notes and appendices.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites this play as another comedy where an item crucial to the plot is fished from the sea, illustrating a common motif.

book:55427.description:
This labyrinthine and extraordinary book, first published more than fifty years ago, was the outcome of Graves's vast reading and curious research into strange territories of folklore, mythology, religion and magic. Erudite and impassioned, it is a scholar-poet's quest for the meaning of European myths, a polemic about the relations between man and woman, and also an intensely personal document in which Graves explored the sources of his own inspiration and, as he believed, all true poetry.
This new edition...
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Graves's book as a learned exposition of the cyclical symbolism associated with a female archetype.

book:46787.description: The narrative drive of Stowe's classic novel is often overlooked in the heat of the controversies surrounding its anti-slavery sentiments. In fact, it is a compelling adventure story with richly drawn characters and has earned a place in both literary and American history. Stowe's puritanical religious beliefs show up in the novel's final, overarching theme--the exploration of the nature of Christianity and how Christian theology is fundamentally incompatible with slavery.
commentaries: Northrop Frye references Stowe's novel as an example where the plot serves to illustrate a central theme, specifically slavery.
Harold Bloom mentions that Tolstoy preferred 'Uncle Tom's Cabin' over Shakespeare's 'King Lear', and suggests modern critical schools would agree.

book:1205517.description: The gods of Olympus died with the advent of Christianity - or so we have been taught to believe. But how are we to account for their tremendous popularity during the Renaissance? This illustrated book, now reprinted in a new, larger paperback format, offers the general reader a multifaceted look at the far-reaching role played by mythology in Renaissance intellectual and emotional life. After a discussion of mythology in late antiquity and the Middle Ages, Jean Seznec traces the fate of the gods from Bottic...
commentaries: Northrop Frye references this book as a source for allegorical explanations of myths.

book:141312.description: Mark Twain's brilliant 19th-century novel has long been recognized as one of the finest examples of American literature. It brings back the irrepressible and free-spirited Huck, first introduced in The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, and puts him center stage. Rich in authentic dialect, folksy humor, and sharp social commentary, Twain's classic tale follows Huck and the runaway slave Jim on an exciting journey down the Mississippi.
commentaries: Northrop Frye uses Huckleberry Finn to discuss the theme of freeing a slave and the ironic recognition scene in comedy.

L'amore per la sapienza, l'immortalita dell'anima, l'autentica nobilta: sono solo alcuni dei temi che Dante tratta nel Convivio, tra il 1304 e il 1307, quando ormai e in esilio.
Nato in una situazione esistenziale particolarmente difficile e interrotto con l'inizio della stesura della Commedia, il Convivio e il libro in cui Dante rilegge tutto il proprio passato di uomo e di poeta, sotto la guida della "Gentile Donna", la Filosofia.
