commentaries: Northrop Frye analyzes the imagery in Yeats's poem 'Sailing to Byzantium', linking it to alchemical symbolism.

book:947771.description:
Aged 51, Yeats proposed to 24 year old George Hyde-Lees (1892-68) in 9/16. They wed on 10/20/16. The marriage was successful, with two children, Anne & Michael. Later he may've had affairs, yet she wrote him: "When you are dead, people will talk about your love affairs, but I shall say nothing, for I will remember how proud you were."
Yeats & George practiced automatic writing involving her contacting various 'Instructors'. The spirit guides communicated a complex system of esoteric characters & history whi...
commentaries: Northrop Frye states that Yeats's work is based on cyclical symbolism and associates it with Blake's poem.

book:2080268.description: Rousseau's ideas have influenced almost every major political development of the last two hundred years, and are crucial to an understanding of phenomena as diverse as the French Revolution, modern educational theory, and the contemporary environmental movement. This is reason enough to draw attention to his startlingly alive autobiography. But the Confessions is also among the greatest self-portraits in world literature -which suggests, even more than the impact of Rousseau's thought, the extent to which t...
commentaries: Erich Auerbach references Rousseau's 'Confessions' as an important stylistic model for later realist writers, despite Rousseau's own lack of full realism, due to its attempt to represent personal existence in relation to contemporary life.
Erich Auerbach contrasts Flaubert's artistic principle with Rousseau's statement from his 'Confessions' to illustrate a shift in literary attitude from self-expression to empathetic absorption.
Northrop Frye references Castiglione as the source of the concept of the 'graceful courtier,' which contributes to the thematic meaning of 'grace' in Renaissance comedy.
Erich Auerbach cites Castiglione's book 'Il Cortegiano' as the most famous illustration of the later fusion of Platonism and the courtly ideal.

book:11904650.description: Hardy tells the story of Tess Durbeyfield, a beautiful young woman living with her impoverished family in Wessex, the southwestern English county immortalized by Hardy. After the family learns of their connection to the wealthy d'Urbervilles, they send Tess to claim a portion of their fortune.
commentaries: Northrop Frye references Hardy's Tess as a modern example of tragedy featuring a calumniated woman figure.

book:826917.description:
With an Introduction and Notes by Phillip Mallett, Senior Lecturer in English, University of St Andrews.
Educated beyond her station, Grace Melbury returns to the woodland village of little Hintock and cannot marry her intended, Giles Winterborne. Her alternative choice proves disastrous, and in a moving tale that has vibrant characters, many humorous moments and genuine pathos coupled with tragic irony, Hardy eschews a happy ending.
With characteristic derision, he exposes the cruel indifference of the arc...
commentaries: Harold Bloom contrasts Esther Summerson with Marty South from Hardy's novel The Woodlanders.

book:2237755.description: The satire in this, one of the best known of all Aristophanes' comedies, is directed against the new schools of philosophy, or perhaps we should rather say dialectic, which had lately been introduced, mostly from abroad, at Athens. The doctrines held up to ridicule are those of the 'Sophists'-such men as Thrasymachus from Chalcedon in Bithynia, Gorgias from Leontini in Sicily, Protagoras from Abdera in Thrace, and other foreign scholars and rhetoricians who had flocked to Athens as the intellectual centre o...
commentaries: Northrop Frye references the play as an example of ironic comedy that edges close to mob violence, specifically its conclusion targeting Socrates.

book:18824506.description: Aristophanes son of Philippus, of the deme Cydathenaus, was a comic playwright of ancient Athens. Eleven of his 40 plays survive virtually complete. These, together with fragments of some of his other plays, provide the only real examples of a genre of comic drama known as Old Comedy, and they are used to define the genre. Also known as the Father of Comedy and the Prince of Ancient Comedy, Aristophanes has been said to recreate the life of ancient Athens more convincingly than any other author. His powers....
commentaries: Northrop Frye states that Lysistrata is an ironic parody of the theme of invincible innocence or virginity.
Northrop Frye cites Aristophanes' The Knights as an example of a comedy featuring the theme of rejuvenation of an old man.

book:752906.description:
Lamenting the unwholesome state of human affairs, a pair of adventurers turn their backs on civilization as they know it and unite with the birds to found an idyllic city in the clouds. Among the earliest existing portrayals of a utopian society, this sparkling fantasy by one of antiquity's most brilliant and popular playwrights offers modern audiences and readers a vision of ancient Greek theater at its very finest.
Widely acknowledged as Aristophanes' masterpiece, this rollicking farce follows the two Ath...
commentaries: Northrop Frye praises Aristophanes' play The Birds as a masterpiece balancing heroic and ironic elements.
Northrop Frye cites Aristophanes' play as the earliest surviving European comedy, noting it contains a character type that persists.
Northrop Frye cites Aristophanes' The Acharnians as an early comedy depicting the establishment of a temperate social order on stage.

book:14583504.description: The Frogs tells the story of the god Dionysus, despairing of the state of Athens' tragedians, and allegedly recovering from the disastrous Battle of Arginusae. He travels to Hades to bring Euripides back from the dead. He brings along his slave Xanthias, who is smarter, stronger, more rational, more prudent, and braver than Dionysus.
commentaries: Northrop Frye references Aristophanes's play as an ancient example of the practice of comparing poets, which is being discussed as a critical technique.
Harold Bloom identifies Aristophanes' play 'The Frogs' as the closest model for Goethe's classical Walpurgis Night.

book:71877.description:
Anna Karenina has beauty, social position, wealth, a husband, and an adored son, but her existence seems empty. When she meets the dashing officer Count Vronsky she rejects her marriage and turns to him to fulfill her passionate nature--with devastating results. One of the world's greatest novels, Anna Karenina is both an immortal drama of personal conflict and social scandal and a vivid, richly textured panorama of nineteenth-century Russia.
While previous versions have softened the robust, and sometimes s...
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Tolstoy's novel as an example of how omens are used as a literary device to create symmetry between beginning and end, even in a realistic work, highlighting Northrop Frye's control over design rather than a belief in fate.

book:785751.description:
In 1879 the fifty-one-year-old author of War and Peaceand Anna Kareninacame to believe that he had accomplished nothing and that his life was meaningless.
Marking a shift in his career from the aesthetic to the religious, Tolstoy's Confessionrelates this spiritual crisis, posing the question: Is there any meaning in my life that will not be destroyed by my death? It is a timeless account of an individual's struggle for faith and meaning.
commentaries: Harold Bloom contrasts the storyteller Tolstoy with Harold Bloom of the philosophical work 'Confession'.

book:28010569.description:
This beautiful Penguin Classics clothbound edition of Tolstoy's great novel is translated with an introduction and notes by Anthony Briggs, and with an afterword by Orlando Figes.
At a glittering society party in St Petersburg in 1805, conversations are dominated by the prospect of war. Terror swiftly engulfs the country as Napoleon's army marches on Russia, and the lives of three young people are changed forever. The stories of quixotic Pierre, cynical Andrey and impetuous Natasha interweave with a huge ca...
commentaries: Harold Bloom mentions Tolstoy's novel 'War and Peace' as the work for which Tolstoy reserved the highest aesthetic eminence.

book:28522772.description: This book of mine, "What is Art?" appears now for the first time in its true form. More than one edition has already been issued in Russia, but in each case it has been so mutilated by the "Censor," that I request all who are interested in my views on art only to judge of them by the work in its present shape. The causes which led to the publication of the book--with my name attached to it--in a mutilated form were the following: In accordance with a decision I arrived at long ago,--not to submit my writing...
commentaries: Harold Bloom references Tolstoy's book 'What Is Art?' as the precursor to his essay criticizing Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom references Tolstoy's book 'What Is Art?' as an example of a flawed aesthetic treatise, grouping it with his essay on Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom references Tolstoy's treatise 'What Is Art?' as an example of his moral vision.

book:7142405.description:
Tolstoy's novella blends fiction and historical fact to portray a legendary Avar chieftain who switched sides in the nineteenth-century Russo-Caucasian war. Inspired by the author's military service, Hadji Muradoffers riveting views of warfare and treason, murder and vengeance, and behind-the-scenes political plotting. An uncharacteristically brief story by the creator of War and Peace,it voices Tolstoy's pacifist beliefs.
This novella also provides a compelling depiction of the Caucasus, a mountainous terr...
commentaries: Harold Bloom compares Tolstoy's work to Whitman's and Ibsen's, describing them as Homeric in their extravagance and generosity.
Harold Bloom references Tolstoy's attempt to depict the fusion of being and consciousness in his work 'Hadji Murad'.

book:936788.description: In partnership with the New York Public Library, Doubleday is proud to introduce a very special collector's series of literary masterpieces. Lavishly illustrated with rare archival material from the library's extensive resources, including the renowned Berg collection, these editions will bring the classics to life for a new generation of readers. In addition to original artwork, each volume contains a fascinating selection of unique materials such as handwritten diaries, letters, manuscripts, and notebooks...
commentaries: Northrop Frye lists this novel as an example of a work that parodies romance conventions.
Harold Bloom contrasts Dickens's potential identification with his character to Flaubert's famous statement about Emma Bovary from Madame Bovary.

book:web_2a5eae66.description: A collection of influential essays on literary theory and criticism, particularly known for the essays "The Intentional Fallacy" and "The Affective Fallacy," which argue against judging a literary work based on authorial intention or reader response.
commentaries: Northrop Frye references a specific chapter in Wimsatt and Beardsley's book as the source for the term 'the intentional fallacy.'

book:3079681.description: Shipwrecked and cast adrift. Lemuel Gulliver wakes to find himself on Lilliput. an island inhabited by little people. whose height makes their quarrels over fashion and fame seem ridiculous. His subsequent encounters - with the crude giants of Brobdingnag. the philosophical Houyhnhnms and brutish Yahoos - give Gulliver new. bitter insights into human behaviour. Swifts savage satire views mankind in a distorted hall of mirrors as a diminished. magnified and finally bestial species. presenting us with an unco...
commentaries: Northrop Frye uses Swift's Gulliver's Travels as a key example of a work that is fiction but not a novel, leading into a discussion of its form.

book:1697398.description:
Montaigne's Essays, which are at once the most celebrated and the most permanent of his productions, form a magazine out of which such minds as those of Bacon and Shakespeare did not disdain to help themselves; and, indeed, the Frenchman's literary importance largely results from the share which his mind had in influencing other minds, coeval and subsequent.
Montaigne's Essaysare, in effect, an extended autobiography, the only one ever to be written in this way. Montaigne does not proceed along the line of....
commentaries: Harold Bloom quotes Emerson's praise for Montaigne's 'Essays', describing the work as profoundly alive and vital.
Edward Gibbon notes that Montaigne used the same anecdote in his essay 'On Pedantry'.

book:352175.description: "Lecteur, je suis moi-meme la matiere de mon livre" : c'est ce surprenant aveu de subjectivite qui ouvre l'un des textes les plus modernes de la litterature francaise, quoique l'un des plus anciens. A la mort de son ami La Boetie, Montaigne decide en effet de prendre la plume pour perpetuer leurs discussions si fecondes. Sur ce mode autobiographique, tous les sujets seront abordes, de l'amitie a l'education, de la philosophie a la lecture, de la religion a la mort des hommes. En s'observant lui-meme, Montai...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Montaigne's 'Essais' as providing a just and lively perspective on the Roman spectacles.

book:web_85150db9.description: A prose satire by Elizabethan writer Thomas Nashe, structured as a complaint to the devil about the vices of society, using the framework of the seven deadly sins.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Nashe's work as an example of the encyclopaedic, preaching-based form of low-norm satire.

book:web_cea0b53c.description: A seminal work of psychoanalytic literary criticism by Otto Rank, analyzing the common pattern in myths of heroic figures. The first edition was published in German in 1909 as 'Der Mythus von der Geburt des Helden'.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites this book as a detailed study relevant to the archetypal narrative being discussed.

book:8107537.description: Wittgenstein and the Practice of Philosophyintroduces Wittgenstein's philosophy to senior undergraduates and graduate students. Its pedagogical premise is that the best way to understand Wittgenstein's thought is to take seriously his methodological remarks.
commentaries: Northrop Frye acknowledges a debt to a specific passage in Langer's book for the concept of a 'state of naive induction.'

book:253801.description: Alfred North Whitehead's SCIENCE AND THE MODERN WORLD, originally published in 1925, redefines the concept of modern science. Presaging by more than half a century most of today's cutting-edge thought on the cultural ramifications of science and technology, Whitehead demands that readers understand and celebrate the contemporary, historical, and cultural context of scientific discovery. Taking readers through the history of modern science, Whitehead shows how cultural history has affected science over the a...
commentaries: Northrop Frye references this book in a comparative note on the rise of Ionian and Renaissance science.

book:29220609.description: An English translation of the words of Muhammad who claimed to get them from the angel Gabriel.
commentaries: Northrop Frye presents the Koran as a historical example of oracular, mythical literature emerging from prophetic tradition.

book:1362044.description: Candidenous conte les mesaventures d'un voyageur philosophe qui affronte les horreurs de la guerre et les sanglants caprices de la Nature ; qui connait les desillusions de l'amour et decouvre les turpitudes de ses semblables, faisant a l'occasion l'experience de leurs dangereuses fantaisies. Pourtant si l'homme est un bien mechant animal et si l'existence n'est qu'une cascade de catastrophes, est-ce une raison pour que le heros perde sa serenite et le recit de son allegresse ? Sous la forme d'une ironique f...
commentaries: Northrop Frye contrasts Voltaire's Candide with Rousseau's Emile to illustrate a shift from the novel to another form of fiction.
Erich Auerbach cites Voltaire's 'Candide' as a work that polemically attacks Leibniz's metaphysical optimism.

book:web_37fa0cfe.description: Voltaire's biography of King Charles XII of Sweden, first published in 1731. It is considered one of the foundational works of modern historical writing, blending narrative with philosophical reflection.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Voltaire's history of Charles XII as a source for a historical analogy.

book:web_894f653f.description: Historical work by Voltaire about the reign of Louis XIV of France, considered one of the first modern histories with critical analysis of sources and emphasis on cultural achievements alongside political events.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Voltaire's history to compare the size of the Roman military establishment with that of a modern European monarchy.

book:8166045.description: Urn Burial, one of the most influential essays in Western literature, is now available as a New Directions Pearl. Hydriotaphia, or Urn Burial, is one of the pinnacles of Renaissance scholarship and without doubt one of the great essays in English literature. Beginning with observations on the recent discovery of Roman antiquities in the form of burial urns, Browne's associative mind wanders to elephant graveyards, to pre-Christian cremation ceremonies, and finally to the idea of Christian burial. Browne the...
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Browne's 'Urn Burial' as an example of a prose work that functions as a rhetorical exercise with recurring rhythmic units.

book:12958554.description:
Utopie, das schone Wort vom Nirgend-Ort, hat am Ende dieses Jahrhunderts seinen Zauberklang verloren. Die Welt ist vermessen, der Bericht von einem unentdeckten Ort, an dem sich besser leben lasst, musste heute aus dem Weltall zu uns dringen, um wenigstens minimale Chancen auf Glaubwurdigkeit zu haben.
In dieser Hinsicht hatte es der Londoner Rechtsgelehrte Thomas More vor fast 500 Jahren einfacher. Amerikas Entdeckung lag 24 Jahre zuruck, da schrieb er einen Bericht uber ein Gesprach mit einem Seefahrer, d...
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites More's 'Utopia' as an example of a satirical 'other world' that presents an ideal society but at the cost of abandoning central Christian tenets.
Erich Auerbach notes that Rabelais borrowed the name 'Utopia' from Thomas More's book.

book:817019.description: A failed revolutionary attempt drives the hero of Hudson's novel to seek refuge in the primeval forests of south-western Venezuela. There, in the 'green mansions' of the title, Abel encounters the wood-nymph Rima, the last survivor of a mysterious aboriginal race. The love that flowers between them is soon overshadowed by cruelty and sorrow... One of the acknowledged masters of natural history writing, W. H. Hudson forms an important link between nineteenth-century Romanticism and the twentieth-century ecol...
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Hudson's 'Green Mansions' as an example where conventional imagery (a serpent in a paradisal setting) is used without explicit authorial guidance.

book:8507025.description: One of a series of miniature poetry books, each illustrated with wood engravings, published by The Folio Society between 1991 and 1997. This volume, bound in blue-green moire silk with a gold slip case, contains the poems 'The Garden', 'The Picture of little T. C. in a Prospect of Flowers', 'The Mower against Gardens', 'Damon the Mower', 'The Mower to the Glow-worms', 'The Mower's Song', 'The Garden of Appleton House' and 'To His Coy Mistress', illustrated with nine small wood-engravings by Harry Brockway.
commentaries: Northrop Frye analyzes a specific conventional extension of imagery found in Marvell's poem 'The Garden'.

book:16121473.description: Ammiratore di Dante e devoto amico di Petrarca, Boccaccio si iscrive nella trilogia dei grandi autori italiani del Trecento. Primo capolavoro di prosa narrativa che folgora e conquista la societa dell'Europa moderna, Il Decameron narra le cento novelle che sette gentili fanciulle e tre cortesi giovani, rufugiati sulle colline fiesolane per evitare il contagio della terribile peste che nel 1348 infierisce su Firenze, si raccontano lungo il corso di dieci giornate. Piu di cinquecento opere d'arte dei secoli X...
commentaries: Northrop Frye states that collections like the Decameron, using a symposium device, belong to the contemplative, 'penseroso' phase of romance.
Northrop Frye cites Boccaccio's Decameron as an example of a work of fiction composed of short stories, analogous to the structure of a confession.
Erich Auerbach directly cites Boccaccio's 'The Decameron' as the primary source text being analyzed, providing the original Italian and an English translation.
Harold Bloom identifies Boccaccio's Decameron as the likely model for Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, despite Chaucer never explicitly mentioning it.
Erich Auerbach introduces a novella from Boccaccio's Decameron as an example to analyze, summarizing its plot.
Erich Auerbach uses Boccaccio's Decameron as a chronological reference point, noting that the text under discussion is over a century more recent.
Erich Auerbach contrasts the Franco-Burgundian stories with Boccaccio's work, listing specific stylistic and thematic elements absent from the imitations.

book:web_15c2614d.description: A scholarly work on Latin language and grammar by the Roman polymath Marcus Terentius Varro, originally consisting of 25 books, though only books 5-10 survive in fragmentary form.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Varro's etymological explanation for the Latin word for army, linking it to the concept of exercise.

book:662942.description: D. H. Lawrence visited Etruria in April, 1927. It was his "last pilgrimage". There sprang from it a documentary account which is both literary guide and spiritual testament, a global vision of the Etruscan civilization.
commentaries: Northrop Frye compares a point to remarks made by D. H. Lawrence in his book.

book:332435.description: A sequel to the banned novel, The Rainbow, Women in Lovefollows the tumultuous lives of the Brangwen sisters, Gudrun and Ursula. Turning his keen eye on the nature of love, commitment, passion, and marriage, Lawrence gives us the stories of two intelligent, incisive, and observant women, whose temperamental differences spark an ongoing debate regarding their society and their inner lives. The two very different sisters pursue thrilling, torrid affairs; but their quest for more mature emotional relationships...
commentaries: Harold Bloom places Esther Summerson in a literary tradition culminating in the characters from Lawrence's Women in Love.

book:17333168.description:
Set in the rural midlands of England, The Rainbow revolves around three generations of the Brangwen family over a period of more than sixty years, setting them against the emergence of modern England. When Tom Brangwen marries a Polish widow and adopts her daughter as his own, he is unprepared for the conflict and passion that erupt. Suffused with biblical imagery, The Rainbow addresses searching human issues in a setting of precise and vivid detail.
In The Rainbow, D. H. Lawrence challenged the customary l...
commentaries: Harold Bloom cites Frank Kermode's comparison, mentioning D. H. Lawrence's 'The Rainbow' as a book about marriage in its spiritual aspects.

book:591705.description: Lawrence asserted that 'the proper function of a critic is to save the tale from the artist who created it'. In these highly individual, penetrating essays he has exposed 'the American whole soul' within some of that continent's major works of literature. In seeking to establish the status of writings by such authors as Poe, Melville, Fenimore Cooper and Whitman, Lawrence himself has created a classic work. Studies in Classic American Literature is valuable not only for the light it sheds on eighteenth- and...
commentaries: Harold Bloom cites Lawrence's book as a point of comparison for the ambivalent reaction to Whitman's work.

book:1780421.description: Despite being abandoned by his parents, Tom Jones grows into a gallant and irresistible young man. Most of his time is spent romping through the English countryside, getting himself into all kinds of trouble with his good nature and unquenchable eye for women. After being betrayed by jealous relatives, Tom is exiled from home and must undergo a variety of trials in his quest to be reunited with his one true love and to redeem himself in the eyes of society. Filled with mischief and adventure, this bildungsr...
commentaries: Northrop Frye uses Fielding's novel as an example of a work named for its plot, while noting Fielding's strong thematic interest.
Northrop Frye uses Tom Jones as an example of a hero facing a near-catastrophic crisis before a comic resolution.
Northrop Frye mentions Tom Jones as an example where the word 'history' is used in a literary context, though the term has since broadened beyond literature.
Erich Auerbach quotes Henry Fielding's Tom Jones to illustrate the 18th-century convention of treating contemporary everyday life within a comic or satiric mode, not with tragic seriousness.

book:1427357.description:
This immortal novel of the sea tells the story of a British sailor haunted by a single youthful act of cowardly betrayal. To the white men in Bombay, Calcutta, and Rangoon, Jim is a man of mystery. To the primitive natives deep in the Malayan jungle, he is a god gifted with supernatural powers. To the beautiful half-caste girl who flees to his hut for protection, he is a lord to be feared and loved.
Lord Jim--Conrad's classic portrait of a man's guilt, his search for forgiveness, and his final, tragic redem...
commentaries: Northrop Frye lists this novel as an example of a work that parodies romance conventions.

book:780681.description: 'Nostromo'--though nearly one hundred years old--says as much about today's Latin America as any of the finest recent accounts of that region's turbulent political life.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites this novel as a modern example in the tradition of romance centered on the quest for buried treasure.

book:web_29e8940f.description: A popular science book exploring cosmology and the nature of the universe, arguing for a mathematical rather than mechanical understanding of reality.
commentaries: Northrop Frye references Jeans's book to discuss the shift from a mechanical to a mathematical conception of the universe, using it as an analogy for how literature can contain the world within its own autonomous structure.
Erich Auerbach references a specific passage from Horace's Ars Poetica to illustrate a point about the mixing of tragic and comic styles.

book:7861910.description: This is a pre-1923 historical reproduction that was curated for quality. Quality assurance was conducted on each of these books in an attempt to remove books with imperfections introduced by the digitization process. Though we have made best efforts - the books may have occasional errors that do not impede the reading experience. We believe this work is culturally important and have elected to bring the book back into print as part of our continuing commitment to the preservation of printed works worldwide.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Victor Hugo's 'Légendes des Siècles' as a later French work attempting to combine two encyclopaedic structural tendencies.

book:1619693.description: Des Esseintes : Le heros fin de siecle par excellence ! Cynique, misogyne et romantique a l'extreme. Aristocrate oisif, isole, il se livre a une meditation sur l'existence, l'art, la religion, les femmes... Il fouille l'experience de l'ennui jusqu'a l'ecoeurement. Son acuite intellectuelle de meme que le raffinement de ses sens lui font mepriser le vulgaire tout en eprouvant l'inevitable souffrance d'une sensibilite trop aiguisee.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Huysmans' À Rebours as a sophisticated example of imaginative withdrawal in literature, associated with the final phase of comedy.

book:web_ba83beed.description: A decadent French novel that follows the reclusive aesthete Jean des Esseintes as he retreats from Parisian society to create an artificial world of sensory experiences. It became a seminal work of the Decadent movement and greatly influenced later writers.
commentaries: Erich Auerbach cites Huysmans's novel as an example of an earlier, subjective narrative work.
Erich Auerbach contrasts Proust's narrative structure with Huysmans's novel, which is presented as an example of a strictly unipersonal subjectivism.

book:80080.description:
An enchanting story that has inspired generations of writers, including Boccaccio, Shakespeare, Cervantes and Keats 
Written towards the end of the second century AD, The Golden Asstells the story of the many adventures of a young man whose fascination with witchcraft leads him to be transformed into a donkey. The bewitched Lucius passes from owner to owner - encountering a desperate gang of robbers and being forced to perform lewd 'human' tricks on stage - until the Goddess Isis finally breaks the spell an...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Apuleius's work as a humorous description of the priests of the Syrian goddess.

book:75600.description: The Life of Henry Brulardis the autobiography of one of France's greatest writers, Stendhal, author of The Red and the Blackand The Charterhouse of Parma. Here, writing at white heat and with such ferocious honesty and indignation that his book was to remain unpublishable for more than a century after its composition, Stendhal revisits his unhappy childhood in a stuffy provincial town and bares his rebellious heart. His adored mother, who died when he was only seven; a father devoted only to his own social....
commentaries: Erich Auerbach quotes from chapter 30 of Stendhal's autobiographical work 'Henri Brulard' to illustrate Stendhal's view on the lack of spirit in professional society.
Erich Auerbach cites Stendhal's 'Henri Brulard' chapter 14 to demonstrate Stendhal's self-described internal conflict between republican views and aristocratic instincts.
Erich Auerbach references Stendhal's 'Henri Brulard' chapter 22 to show Stendhal's critical view of post-Revolution cultural decline.
Erich Auerbach references Stendhal's 'Henri Brulard' chapter 32 to note Stendhal's self-description of a sensitive, feminine physical constitution.
Erich Auerbach quotes from Stendhal's 'Henri Brulard' chapter 2 to present Stendhal's occasional socialist-leaning observation on where true energy resides.
Erich Auerbach cites Stendhal's 'Henri Brulard' chapter 26 to analyze Stendhal's materialistic and sensualistic definition of human character as the habitual pursuit of happiness.
Erich Auerbach references Stendhal's 'Henri Brulard' chapter 32 to contrast Stendhal's personal freedom with romantic aversion to bourgeois money-making.

book:2554799.description: Memoirs of an Egotist,Stendhal's fragmentary autobiographical work, is alert, wry, and perpetually self-questioning. Through a series of apparently random impressions of the political, social, and artistic movements of the world around him, he imbues a range of human experience, from the mundane to the extraordinary, with the significance it deserves. Foreword by Doris Lessing. Containing everything from delightful thumbnail sketches of his friends and colleagues, to lyrical remembrances of gardens and oper...
commentaries: Erich Auerbach quotes from Stendhal's 'Souvenirs d'égotisme' chapter 6 to highlight Stendhal's ambivalence and criticism toward his fellow liberals.
Erich Auerbach cites Stendhal's 'Souvenirs d'égotisme' chapter 7 to exemplify Stendhal's aversion to bourgeois provincial merchants.
Erich Auerbach quotes from Stendhal's 'Souvenirs d'égotisme' chapter 1 to reveal Stendhal's admission that fear, not easy mastery, directed a decade of his life, particularly in concealing passion.
Erich Auerbach introduces the character Julien Sorel as the protagonist of Stendhal's novel 'Le Rouge et le Noir'.

book:web_bc2e06b4.description: Philosophical work by Francis Bacon proposing a new system of logic based on inductive reasoning and empirical observation, foundational to the scientific method.
commentaries: Thomas S. Kuhn references Bacon's work as containing a sketch for a natural history of heat.

book:web_325744ee.description: A collection of essays edited by R. S. Crane, containing his influential essay 'The Concept of Plot and the Plot of Tom Jones' along with other works by the Chicago School of criticism.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites Crane's essay in an edited volume for its discussion of plot, specifically in relation to a work being 'named after its plot.'

book:web_23df63b8.description: A collection of lectures by R. S. Crane, a prominent literary critic and leader of the Chicago School of literary criticism, focusing on critical methods and poetic structure.
commentaries: Northrop Frye acknowledges a substantial debt to Crane's book for the theory of the formal phase of criticism.

book:web_b93f8d4d.description: A study examining Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's relationship with and influence on music, including his collaborations with composers and his theories about musical aesthetics.
commentaries: Northrop Frye cites this book for a specific conception of 'parody' in a context where little has been said on a topic.

book:6492522.description:
One of the most significant works of literary criticism of this century, Erich Auerbach's Mimesisundertakes a new and profound approach to major moments in Western literature. More than a work of literary criticism, this study is filled with insights into the Western imagination and Western culture itself, in its repeated attempts to master and control reality and experience.

book:19168304.description: German classicist's monumental study of the origins of European thought in Greek literature and philosophy. Brilliant, widely influential. book:75495.description: Begun in 1923 and published 1930, The Bridgeis Crane's major work. "Very roughly," he wrote a friend, "it concerns a mystical synthesis of 'America' . . .
