book:web_a49de2b9.description: A collection of short stories by Isaac Babel about Jewish gangsters in the Moldavanka district of Odessa, featuring the character Benya Krik. The stories were written and published in the 1920s-1930s, with the first English translation appearing in 1955.
commentaries: Harold Bloom references Isaak Babel as the writer of a specific book, 'Tales of Odessa', noting its thematic connection to Borges's story.

book:web_f0a20019.description: A critical study examining modern playwrights as intellectual figures, focusing on dramatists like Ibsen, Strindberg, Shaw, and Brecht.
commentaries: Harold Bloom references Bentley's book as a conceptual model for a hypothetical volume on poets as thinkers, using it to frame Dickinson's significance.

book:web_5a1dfdd7.description: A memoir and critical study by Frank Budgen, a friend and contemporary of James Joyce, detailing Joyce's creative process and personal insights during the writing of 'Ulysses'.
commentaries: Harold Bloom cites Budgen's book as the best guide to Joyce's 'Ulysses' and quotes its insight about Joyce's focus on Shakespeare the man.

book:web_1bd0f82d.description: A scholarly work examining rhetorical theory and its historical development, applying critical theory to the study of rhetoric.
commentaries: Harold Bloom cites de Bolla's book to support a critique of Freudian interpretations of literary influence.

book:web_fa9d5cb7.description: A scholarly work applying Wittgenstein's philosophy to the tragic sense of life in Samuel Johnson and Percy Bysshe Shelley.
commentaries: Harold Bloom cites Quinney's book as a study applying Wittgenstein's ideas to other literary figures.

book:web_081cec55.description: A scholarly work examining Shakespeare's engagement with and adaptation of Chaucer's works, focusing on literary parallels and influences.
commentaries: Harold Bloom cites Donaldson's book to support the analysis of parallels between Shakespeare's and Chaucer's characters, specifically regarding their absorption in play.

book:757090.description: Eusebius' Ecclesiastical History is one of the classics of early Christianity and of equal stature with the works of Flavius Josephus. Eusebius chronicles the events of the first three centuries of the Christian church in such a way as to record a vast number of vital facts about early Christianity that can be learned from no other ancient source. When Eusebius wrote his Ecclesiastical History, his vital concern was to record facts before they disappeared, and before eye-witnesses were killed and libraries....
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History, which quotes the letters of Bishop Dionysius, as the source for demographic data from Alexandria.

book:20087887.description: Written in the early fourth century BCE by a gentleman and soldier from Athens, "Cyropaedia" is an account of Cyrus the Great that escapes a simple genre placement. It is a sort of historical, political, biographical, fictional romance, encapsulating the sweeping type of narrative characteristic of Xenophon's works. The overall portrait of Cyrus is artistic, offering glimpses of this huge figure's character. Organized into eight books, the entire life of Cyrus the Great is told, from his descent and educati...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon critiques the portrayal of Alexander Severus in the Augustan History as a poorly executed imitation of Xenophon's Cyropaedia.

book:20657855.description: In The Persian Expedition, Xenophon, a young Athenian noble who sought his destiny abroad, provides an enthralling eyewitness account of the attempt by a Greek mercenary army - the Ten Thousand - to help Prince Cyrus overthrow his brother and take the Persian throne. When the Greeks were then betrayed by their Persian employers, they were forced to march home through hundreds of miles of difficult terrain - adrift in a hostile country and under constant attack from the unforgiving Persians and warlike tribe...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Xenophon's Anabasis as a source in a footnote regarding the location or description of Trebizond.
Edward Gibbon cites Xenophon's work to provide historical detail on Persian military practices, specifically the encampment distance of their cavalry.

book:web_13f33ed4.description: A collection of short chapters on grammar, philosophy, history, antiquarianism, and other subjects, preserving fragments of many authors and works that otherwise might be unknown.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Aulus Gellius's Attic Nights to support a point about the status of municipal cities and colonies during the reign of Hadrian.
Edward Gibbon references Minutius Faelix's work 'Octavio' as a source.

book:8254877.description: The emperor Marcus Aurelius, the proverbial philosopher-king, produced in Greek a Roman manual of piety, the Meditations, whose impact has been felt for ages since. Here, for our age, is his great work presented in its entirety, strongly introduced and freshly, elegantly translated.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Marcus Aurelius's own work, 'Meditations', to illustrate the emperor's personal and favorable view of his wife's character.

book:13809066.description:
A classic of the ancient world of warfare
De Re Militari (Concerning Military Affairs), written in the 5th century by Vegetius and translated from the original Latin, is a treatise on warfare in the Roman world and is vital reading for any modern student of the subject as it clearly outlines the methods and practices of the type of warfare waged by the Roman Empire at the height of its power. So influential was Vegetius' book that it was considered as an essential field-guide well into the age of gunpowder....
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Vegetius's work on military matters as a source for information on the Roman legion.
Edward Gibbon cites Vegetius's work on military matters, noting it as an abridgment of regulations from the time of Trajan and Hadrian.
Edward Gibbon references Vegetius's work for a linguistic point about the term 'miles' in different historical periods.
Edward Gibbon cites Vegetius's work on military science to provide evidence about the cavalry composition of the Imperial legion.

book:1729258.description: From a small Iron-Age settlement on the banks of the Tiber, Rome grew to become the centre of an empire that dominated what was then known of the western world. This book recreates the evolution of that city, describing the individuals and events that made Rome a political and cultural conqueror. The book portrays not only the cynosures of the Roman world, but also lesser known figures, reassessing their impact upon both the character of Roman society and the development of the Empire. Rome's artistic achie...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Mr. Wotton's 'History of Rome' to correct a misinterpretation of Dion's text regarding military classifications.
Edward Gibbon references Mr. Wotton's historical work to support the description of public joy at Commodus's return.
Edward Gibbon references Wotton's work to provide an etymological explanation for the name Elagabalus.

book:9989867.description: This is a reproduction of a book published before 1923. This book may have occasional imperfections such as missing or blurred pages, poor pictures, errant marks, etc. that were either part of the original artifact, or were introduced by the scanning process. We believe this work is culturally important, and despite the imperfections, have elected to bring it back into print as part of our continuing commitment to the preservation of printed works worldwide. We appreciate your understanding of the imperfect...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Athenaeus's 'Deipnosophist' as a source, citing a specific edition.

book:web_90fc3010.description: A comprehensive history of the Jewish people from ancient times to the early 18th century, written by French Protestant historian Jacques Basnage. First published in Rotterdam in 1706-1707.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Basnage's history of the Jews concerning the persecution of Jews and Christians.
Edward Gibbon references Basnage's 'Histoire des Juifs' as a source for information on Maimonides's teachings.

book:web_d08910b9.description: A foundational work of historical geography describing ancient Germany, its peoples, and Roman interactions. Published in Leiden.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon again references Cluver's work for traces of old tribal names, indicating it as a source for antiquarian information.
Edward Gibbon cites Cluverius's antiquarian work as an authority on the geographical features of ancient Germany.
Edward Gibbon references Cluver's 'Germania Antiqua' as an authority on ancient Germanic antiquities.
Edward Gibbon directs the reader to Cluver's work for further information on the ancient geography of Germany.
Edward Gibbon references Cluver's work as a source for geographical and historical information about ancient Germany.

book:web_57a4c4eb.description: A foundational work of historical geography describing ancient Italy, its regions, peoples, and antiquities. Clüver (often Latinized as Cluverius) was an early modern geographer and historian.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Cluver's work 'Italia Antiqua' as a geographical source.

book:web_b59de6dd.description: A Latin didactic poem on hunting, written by the Roman poet Nemesianus in the 3rd century AD. The work consists of 325 hexameters and was dedicated to the emperors Carinus and Numerian.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Nemesian's Cynegeticon as a source regarding expectations for the Roman campaign against Persia.
Edward Gibbon references Nemesian's Cynegeticon again, noting his poetic account of Carinus's personal courage in the Gallic war.

book:web_c0f63cfa.description: A collection of dissertations on the Roman lex regia (royal law) by Gerard Noodt and Jacob Gronovius, published in Leiden in 1731.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon lists the dissertations of Noodt and Gronovius as consulted modern works.

book:web_1408c17f.description: A multi-volume history of the German people by the German historian Heinrich Luden (1778-1847). The citation 'Geschichte des T. V.' is a common abbreviation for 'Geschichte des teutschen Volkes' (History of the Teutonic/German People). Volume 1 was published in 1825.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Luden's historical work for a specific interpretation regarding the structure of Tacitus's 'Germania'.
Edward Gibbon notes Luden's patriotic defense of ancient German virtues in his history.

book:web_1726a5da.description: A speech of praise delivered by Pliny the Younger to Emperor Trajan in 100 AD, later published as a model of panegyric oratory. It celebrates Trajan's virtues and contrasts him favorably with previous emperors like Domitian.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Pliny's 'Panegyric' as a factual source on Trajan's education and talents.
Edward Gibbon mentions Pliny's Panegyric as a source on the mildness and precision of tax laws under Trajan and the Antonines.

book:2986217.description: Justin Martyr was one of the Fathers of the Church, born in Sichem, Samaria. He was converted to Christianity, studied Stoic and Platonic philosophy, and founded a school of Christian philosophy at Rome, where he wrote two Apologies on Christian belief (150-60). He is said to have been martyred at Rome. Curiosity is baffled, but faith and love are fed by these scanty relics of primitive antiquity. Yet may we well be grateful for what we have. These writings come down to us as the earliest response of conver...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon quotes Justin Martyr's Apology to show that Christians were willing to serve in secular matters other than worship.

book:web_f610ffe1.description: A major historical work by Carlo Denina tracing the political and cultural revolutions of Italy across centuries. The full Italian title is 'Delle rivoluzioni d'Italia' (often abbreviated as 'Revol. d'Italia'). The cited edition is likely a later 18th or early 19th century edition.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon suggests comparing Maffei's view with Denina's work on the revolutions of Italy.
Edward Gibbon quotes Denina's observation from 'delle Revoluz. d' Italia' regarding the policies of different states towards citizenship.

book:web_dc40796e.description: Collection of orations by the Greek sophist and rhetorician Libanius of Antioch. 'Oratio i' refers to the first oration in his collected works.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Libanius as providing corroborating testimony on the succession of Constantine.

book:6045475.description: "'Geographica' potrebbe essere considerato il punto di partenza di un viaggio alla scoperta di un viaggio alla scoperta del mondo da parte di ciascun lettore. Il nostro viaggio ha inizio dall'originale dell'universo e della nascita della Terra, il pianeta vivente. Terra, acqua e atmosfera forniscono il nutrimento per la complessa evoluzione degli organismi viventi culminata nella comparsa dell'uomo. La storia geologica, influenzata dalle mutevoli forze naturali, fa posto poco alla volta ai documenti della s...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Strabo's Geography as a source of geographical information.
Edward Gibbon cites Strabo's 'Geographica' as a source for geographical and historical information about the Marcomanni.

book:web_67088bc0.description: A scholarly treatise on ancient Roman currency and monetary systems by the Dutch classical scholar Jacobus Gronovius (1645-1716). The work analyzes the value, denominations, and historical context of Roman money.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Gronovius's work 'de Pecunia Veteri' to calculate the increase in Praetorian pay under Domitian.

book:web_b552d7fa.description: A dissertation on the 'lex regia' (royal law) concerning the transfer of power from the Roman people to the emperor, published in Leiden. Often bound with or referenced alongside the dissertations of Noodt on the same topic.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon lists the dissertations of Noodt and Gronovius as consulted modern works.
Edward Gibbon cites Lactantius as a source of evidence regarding the choice of Constantine by his dying father.
Edward Gibbon directs the reader to Lactantius for details on the financial inquisition and use of torture under Galerius.
Edward Gibbon cites Lactantius as a partial and injudicious source for an anecdote about a private conversation between Diocletian and Galerius, questioning its truth and decency.
Edward Gibbon quotes Lactantius to describe the rapid and improbable promotion of Maximin from humble origins to the rank of Caesar.
Edward Gibbon acknowledges Lactantius as a source that even praises the diligence and fidelity of the emperor Severus.
Edward Gibbon attributes a report about Galerius's long-term imperial schemes to Lactantius, while casting strong doubt on its reliability.

book:web_c7a2cf45.description: A theological work by Lactantius, also known as 'Divine Institutes', written in the early 4th century AD. It is an apologetic work defending Christianity against pagan critics and explaining Christian doctrine.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Lactantius's 'Divine Institutes' as a source describing prophecies of future calamities with eloquence.

book:web_963ee61e.description: Also known as 'Lives of the Sophists', this work by Philostratus of Lemnos (c. 170–247/250 AD) contains biographies of famous sophists from the 5th century BC to his own time. The reference 'l. ii. p. 548' indicates Book 2, page 548 of the Olearius edition.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Philostratus's Lives of the Sophists as a source.

book:web_87ab4caf.description: A two-volume history of the German people from ancient times to the early 19th century.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Greenwood's history as an additional source noting the inclusion of the Salii and Cherasci in the Frankish confederation.

book:web_2ee85205.description: A satirical work by Roman Emperor Julian the Apostate, in which Roman emperors debate their merits at a banquet in heaven.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references a work by Julian (the Emperor Julian) containing a speech of Augustus.

book:web_48c496f6.description: First oration by Julian the Apostate, Roman Emperor and philosopher, written in Greek as part of his rhetorical works defending paganism and criticizing Christianity.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon includes Julian's oration as part of the evidence supporting the narrative of Constantine's designation.

book:web_c04146f4.description: Satirical work by Roman Emperor Julian (the Apostate), also known as 'The Caesars' or 'Symposium of the Caesars', written around 362 AD. It depicts a banquet where Roman emperors compete before the gods.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Julian's work 'The Caesars', with observations by Spanheim, on Dacian beliefs.
Edward Gibbon references Julian's work 'Caesares' as a source for representing Trajan's sentiments in a just and lively manner.
Edward Gibbon references Julian's work 'Caesares' as a source on Roman emperors.
Edward Gibbon references Julian's work, noting his use of an image and critiquing his interpretation.
Edward Gibbon references Julian's critical opinion on the severity of Emperor Probus.
Edward Gibbon references Julian's work 'The Caesars' to report Constantine's claim of recovering Dacia.
Edward Gibbon references Julian as a source of criticisms against early Christians, noting that his accusations are discussed alongside a defense by church fathers.

book:web_7273e12c.description: A major historical work by the English scholar and clergyman Humphrey Prideaux, connecting biblical history with secular history of the ancient Near East. It was highly influential in 18th-century biblical scholarship.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Prideaux's 'Connection' as a source for information on the Herodians.

book:web_4d05b38e.description: A historical and theological treatise on the practice of tithing, written by the English churchman and scholar Humphrey Prideaux (1648–1724). It was first published in 1681 and was a significant work in the debates over ecclesiastical revenues.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Prideaux's work as a source to consult on the subject of tithes and ecclesiastical revenues.

book:web_7b92016b.description: Michaelis's comprehensive work on Mosaic law, originally published in German. The English translation referenced in Gibbon's footnote is 'Commentaries on the Laws of Moses' (1814).
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Michaelis's work to present an explanation that Moses, as a civil legislator, focused on temporal sanctions and avoided threats of otherworldly punishments.

book:web_c8dec8d6.description: A universal chronicle translated and extended by Jerome from the earlier chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea, covering world history from Abraham to his own time. Often cited in historical scholarship as 'Hieronymus, Chronicon' or abbreviated 'Hieronym. in Chron.'
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Hieronym (Jerome) as a source for the narrative of Numerian's death.

book:web_68a02451.description: Major historical work by Tacitus covering the Roman Empire from the death of Augustus (14 AD) to the death of Domitian (96 AD). The work is commonly referred to as 'Annals' and was written circa 110 AD.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's 'Annal.' as a source for the description of a battle, drawing a parallel between the Gothic conflict and a similar engagement recorded by the Roman historian.
Edward Gibbon references Tacitus's 'Annals' as a historical source.

book:web_81c81478.description: A major historical work on early Christianity before Constantine by the influential church historian Johann Lorenz von Mosheim. The abbreviated citation 'De Reb. Christ.' refers to this Latin treatise.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Mosheim's work to support the note that the Millennial tradition is of Jewish origin.

book:web_447ff721.description: Mosheim's seminal work on ecclesiastical history, commonly known in English as 'Ecclesiastical History, Ancient and Modern' or 'General History of the Church'. It was first published in Latin in 1755 and became a standard reference work, with numerous translations and editions throughout the 18th and 19th centuries.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon directs the reader to Mosheim's work for information on historical parallels regarding donations motivated by the approaching end of the world.

book:831106.description: Edward Gibbon called The Historiesan 'immortal work, every sentence of which is pregnant with the deepest observations and the most lively images.' Its author, Cornelius Tacitus, widely acknowledged as the greatest of all Roman historians, describes with cynical power the murderous 'Year of the Four Emperors' - AD 69 - when in just a few months the whole of the Roman Empire was torn apart by civil war. The ultimate triumph of Vespasian and his sons Titus and Domitian was only the prelude to further conflict...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Tacitus's Histories in a footnote regarding the security of frontier camps in a more prosperous age.

book:30478027.description: This work has been selected by scholars as being culturally important, and is part of the knowledge base of civilization as we know it. This work was reproduced from the original artifact, and remains as true to the original work as possible. Therefore, you will see the original copyright references, library stamps (as most of these works have been housed in our most important libraries around the world), and other notations in the work.This work is in the public domain in the United States of America, and....
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's work 'Agricola' to support an observation about an inherent defect.

book:15781142.description: Die "Germania" des Tacitus setzt sich mit dem Leben bei den Germanen seiner Zeit auseinander. Er gibt somit einen guten Einblick in die Lebensverhaltnisse und die Lebensumstande bei den Germanen des 1. Jahrhunderts nach Christus. Er ist die einzige Quelle, die aus dieser Zeit berichtet und daher ist es eher schade, dass man so erhebliche Abstriche an seiner Genauigkeit machen muss. Tacitus verfolgte mit seiner Schrift namlich vornehmlich ein Ziel, und zwar den Romern, die zu seinen Lebzeiten bereits sehr de...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's 'Germania' as a source regarding amber.
Edward Gibbon notes that Tacitus's 'Germania' has been extensively analyzed and interpreted by later historians.
Edward Gibbon quotes Tacitus's 'Germania' to describe the physical stature and constitution of the ancient Germans.
Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's 'Germania' as a source for information about the Germans.
Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's 'Germania' as the source for a description of Roman policy towards the Germans, and notes that the Abbé de la Bléterie criticized Tacitus's sentiments.
Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's 'Germania' as a source for the claim that the inhabitants of Sweden had large vessels with oars.
Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's 'Germania' as an authority on the military equipment and political obedience of the Germanic tribes.
Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's 'Germania' as a source for geographical or ethnographic details about the Germanic tribes.
Edward Gibbon cites specific chapters of Tacitus' Germania as a source on the characteristics of the Germanic tribes.
Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's 'Germania' as a source for information about Germanic tribes.

book:15808557.description:
A compelling new translation of a vital account of Roman history
With clarity and vivid intensity, Tacitus's Annalsrecounts the pivotal events in Roman history from the years shortly before the death of Augustus to the death of Nero in 68 AD, including the reign of terror under the corrupt Tiberius, the great fire of Rome during the time of Nero, and the wars, poisonings, scandals, conspiracies, and murders that were part of imperial life. Despite Tacitus's claim that they were written objectively, the Anna...
commentaries: Erich Auerbach introduces a passage from Tacitus' Annals as a specimen of ancient historiography to analyze its representation of historical forces.
Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's Annals as a historical source.
Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's Annals as a source for details about the execution of Agrippina and Tiberius's response.
Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's Annals again for an anecdote about a failed escape attempt under Tiberius.
Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's 'Annales' as a source for historical information about the Marcomanni and their king Maroboduus.
Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's Annals as a source, referencing a specific book and section.
Edward Gibbon cites a specific book by Tacitus as a source for the account of the slaughter of Varus and his legions.
Edward Gibbon references the second book of Tacitus's Annals for further historical details.
Edward Gibbon cites Tacitus's 'Annals' as a source for a speech by Tiberius.
Edward Gibbon references Tacitus's 'Annals' to support the dating of the Goths' establishment near the Vistula.

book:web_c97ff121.description: Historical work by Tacitus covering the Roman Empire from 69-96 AD, originally comprising 12-14 books (only Books 1-4 and part of Book 5 survive).
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Tacitus's historical work as the source for the account of the Batavian revolt, critiquing its literary style.

book:web_8e2c2db2.description: A dialogue by Lucian of Samosata praising friendship, in which a Scythian named Toxaris recounts stories of Scythian heroes and their war against the Bosporan Kingdom.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Lucian's 'Toxaris' as a literary source for a historical conflict, while noting its potentially fictional character.

book:web_cb23b6b8.description: Second book in Clement of Alexandria's trilogy, following the 'Protrepticus' and preceding the 'Stromata'. It presents Christ as the divine instructor teaching Christians how to live ethically. The work covers practical morality, daily conduct, and Christian lifestyle.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references this work as containing the foundational principles of ethics taught in prominent Christian schools.

book:web_18e891fd.description: A patriotic work by Swedish scholar Olaus Rudbeck that argued Sweden was the lost civilization of Atlantis, the origin of Greek culture, and the cradle of European civilization. Published in Latin as 'Atland eller Manheim'.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Rudbeck's work 'Atlantica' as an example of an antiquarian system that ascribes all celebrated history and fable to Sweden, but notes this system is annihilated by a single fact.

book:web_a318e54e.description: A comprehensive ecclesiastical history by Jean Le Clerc (Johannes Clericus), a Swiss theologian and biblical scholar. The work covers early church history and was influential in Enlightenment-era religious scholarship.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Le Clerc's 'Ecclesiastical History' for information on the church of Pella retaining the title of Jerusalem.

book:web_2c56ce92.description: A Byzantine world chronicle covering history from creation to 1057 CE, compiled by Georgius Cedrenus in the 11th-12th century. The work is often cited in historical scholarship by its Latin title 'Compendium Historiarum' or simply as 'Cedrenus'.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Cedrenus as another source mentioning the Roman embassy.

book:web_9513f162.description: A philosophical dialogue by Montesquieu in which the Roman dictator Sulla converses with Eucrates, exploring themes of power, ambition, and historical legacy.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon praises Montesquieu's work for its eloquent portrayal of a historical figure's perspective.
Edward Gibbon references Montesquieu's 'The Spirit of the Laws' in a footnote discussing the pernicious method of tax collection.

book:436352.description: Ptolemy's Almagest is one of the most influential scientific works in history. A masterpiece of technical exposition, it was the basic textbook of astronomy for more than a thousand years, and still is the main source for our knowledge of ancient astronomy. This translation, based on the standard Greek text of Heiberg, makes the work accessible to English readers in an intelligible and reliable form. It contains numerous corrections derived from medieval Arabic translations and extensive footnotes that take...
commentaries: Thomas S. Kuhn cites this work as a classic that defined legitimate problems and methods for a research field, serving a function similar to modern textbooks.

book:web_950243cb.description: A universal chronicle in two parts: the Chronographia (comparative tables of historical chronologies) and the Chronikoi Kanones (synchronized timeline of events). Originally written in Greek, it survives mainly through Jerome's Latin translation and Armenian fragments.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Eusebius's chronicle as a historical source for details about the plague and depopulation.

book:web_60b60ec7.description: Biography of Roman Emperor Constantine the Great, written by Eusebius of Caesarea, a Christian historian and bishop. The work is a panegyric that presents Constantine as an ideal Christian ruler and provides important historical details about his reign and the early Christianization of the Roman Empire.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon uses Eusebius's work on the life of Constantine as an authoritative source for historical details.

book:web_fba5fb01.description: A seminal work on Roman military organization, tactics, and equipment by the classical scholar Justus Lipsius. It was highly influential in early modern military thought and antiquarian studies of ancient Rome.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon directs the reader to Lipsius's work for detailed information on Roman legionary arms.

book:web_2fa81959.description: A treatise on the greatness of ancient Rome, focusing on its population, military strength, and urban dimensions. Part of Lipsius's antiquarian scholarship on Roman civilization.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon again cites Lipsius's work, this time for information on the Roman navy.
Edward Gibbon directs the reader to Lipsius's work for further information on the size and organization of the Roman military.
Edward Gibbon cites Lipsius's book 'de magnitudine Romana' for numerical details about the Praetorian Guard.
Edward Gibbon references Lipsius's work as providing a scholarly defense of a textual interpretation related to Constantine's birth.

book:web_eb4ca4bb.description: A treatise by the renowned humanist Justus Lipsius on the pronunciation of the Latin language, arguing for a reconstructed classical pronunciation over the medieval ecclesiastical one.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Lipsius's specific work on Latin pronunciation by chapter in a footnote.

book:web_b5405c13.description: A late Roman historical work, often called the 'Breviary of Rufus' or 'Breviarium Rufi', summarizing Roman history and military victories. The author is traditionally identified as Sextus Rufus, a 4th-century Roman official.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Sextus Rufus's work to support the characterization of Odenathus's forces and origins.

book:web_7d11294a.description: A comprehensive historical work on the progressive extension of Roman citizenship and rights to Latium, Italy, and the provinces, tracing the expansion of the Roman political community.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon describes Spanheim's 'Orbis Romanus' as a comprehensive historical work on the extension of Roman citizenship.

book:web_accb79ae.description: A collection of biographies of Roman emperors, heirs, and usurpers from 117 to 284 AD, traditionally attributed to six authors (the 'Scriptores Historiae Augustae'), though its authorship, date, and purpose are contested by modern scholarship.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites the Augustan History as a reference for the tax policies and legal protections of the Roman Empire.

book:web_1227203d.description: A monumental 44-volume encyclopedia of natural history, published between 1749-1804, covering all known aspects of the natural world with detailed descriptions and illustrations.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Buffon's natural history work to provide supporting information on the height of the Peak of Tenerife and its potential notice by ancient peoples.
Edward Gibbon cites Buffon's work as a source for natural historical information, specifically referenced in a footnote.
Edward Gibbon references Buffon's natural history work for comparative mortality tables to analyze the demographic data from Alexandria.
Edward Gibbon cites Buffon's work as a source of natural history information regarding the ostrich.
Edward Gibbon references Buffon's work to note its limitations in describing the giraffe.

book:web_43c31930.description: A topographical and historical work on ancient Rome by the Italian scholar Bernardinus Donatus, first published in 1638. It describes the monuments and ruins of ancient Rome and was an important Renaissance antiquarian text.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Donatus's book as a source on the public monuments and edifices of ancient Rome.

book:web_8bf4be26.description: Historical work by Josephus describing the First Jewish-Roman War (66-73 CE), originally written in Aramaic and later translated to Greek. The Latin title 'De Bello Judaico' was commonly used in European scholarship.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Josephus's work as the source for a footnote describing an oration as a fine picture of the Roman empire.
Edward Gibbon cites Josephus's work on the Jewish War for demographic information about Egypt.

book:web_d5d6f33b.description: A legal and historical treatise on Roman imperial power by the Italian jurist and scholar Giovanni Vincenzo Gravina. It was published as part of his collected works (Opuscula).
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Gravina's work from his Opuscula as a consulted modern source.

book:web_ffd3f191.description: Classical Armenian history attributed to Moses of Chorene (Movses Khorenatsi), a 5th-century historian considered the 'father of Armenian history.' The work chronicles Armenian history from legendary origins to the 5th century AD.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Moses of Chorene as another historian providing a different date for the event, illustrating the chronological discrepancies.
Edward Gibbon references Moses of Chorene's historical work in a footnote about the destruction of temples.
Edward Gibbon cites Moses of Chorene as a source for details about Tiridates' physical strength and education.
Edward Gibbon cites Moses of Chorene's Armenian history regarding the destruction of Armenian religious statues and altars by Persian conquerors.

book:web_8e982690.description: A major apologetic work by Tertullian, defending Christianity against Roman persecution and accusations of disloyalty. Written around 197 AD, it argues for religious freedom and presents Christian beliefs systematically.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Tertullian's apologetic works to illustrate early Christian views on idolatry and public life.

book:web_f6621980.description: Early Christian treatise by Tertullian defending a Christian soldier who refused to wear a laurel crown during military ceremonies, arguing that such pagan symbols were incompatible with Christian faith.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Tertullian's treatise 'De Corona' as a defense of a Christian soldier's act of discarding a laurel crown, discussing its historical context.
Edward Gibbon references Tertullian's treatise to discuss the early Christian attitude toward military service and the suggestion of desertion.

book:web_2b1dabbb.description: A scholarly treatise on Roman taxes and public revenues, compiled from classical sources by the Dutch philologist Pieter Burman the Elder (1668-1741). The work is often cited in 18th-19th century classical scholarship.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Burman's work 'de Vectigal' (On Taxes) in a footnote concerning Roman taxation.

book:web_39c8b369.description: A monumental multi-volume history of Italy from ancient times to the 18th century, written by the Italian historian and scholar Lodovico Antonio Muratori. The first edition was published in 12 volumes between 1744 and 1749.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Muratori's historical work to present a scholarly opinion on seasonal details, while also critiquing it.

book:web_b1a84e2b.description: Historical work by Abbé Dubos arguing for the continuity of Gallic institutions under Roman rule and into the Frankish monarchy.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Dubos's historical work, critiquing its unsuccessful argument about the continuity of Gallic assemblies under Roman rule.

book:web_ad885b0f.description: A philosophical history analyzing the factors behind the rise and fall of the Roman Empire, written by the influential French Enlightenment thinker Montesquieu.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Montesquieu's work to support an observation about the lack of fortified cities and independent power bases in the Roman Empire.
Edward Gibbon paraphrases and discusses Montesquieu's analysis of the Roman military government as an irregular republic.

book:web_980c7b27.description: A pioneering work on ancient Persian religion and Zoroastrianism by Oxford scholar Thomas Hyde. The title is commonly abbreviated as 'De Religione Persarum' (On the Religion of the Persians).
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Hyde's work on Persian religion regarding the life and actions of Zoroaster.
Edward Gibbon cites Hyde's work again in a later footnote regarding Persian religion.

book:web_43991c42.description: Roman historical work covering the period from the Trojan War to AD 30, written by Velleius Paterculus, a Roman historian and soldier. The work is also known as 'Roman History' or 'Compendium of Roman History'.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Velleius Paterculus's 'Historiae Romanae' as a source for historical information about the Marcomanni and their king Maroboduus.

book:web_9ffdfecf.description: A series of lectures on ancient and modern literature delivered by Friedrich Schlegel in Vienna, 1812, and first published posthumously in 1815.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Schlegel's work to present the theory that Runic characters originated with the Phoenicians.

book:web_23b1cf2c.description: A historical and genealogical account of the Mongols and Tatars, written by the Khan of Khiva. First published in a French translation in 1726, with an English translation appearing later.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references this work in a footnote as another example of a tradition tracing a nation's lineage back to a son of Japhet, similar to the Irish case.

book:web_2778d1a8.description: A major history of Italy from 1789 to 1814, published in multiple volumes. The first edition appeared in 1824, with subsequent volumes published later. Gibbon's citation refers to Volume XIV.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Botta's history of Italy as a source for the historical note on the end of Corsican struggles for independence.

book:web_8ee8d92a.description: A foundational history of Roman law by the German jurist and legal scholar Johann Gottlieb Heineccius, first published in 1733. It was a standard reference work on Roman legal history throughout the 18th and 19th centuries.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon directs the reader to Heineccius's work on Roman law for further information on Papinian.

book:web_eb34e9f2.description: A pioneering historical and archaeological study of the Roman road system, its construction, and its administration. Bergier was a French lawyer, scholar, and antiquarian.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Bergier's 'Histoire des grands Chemins de l'Empire Romain' as a source on the construction of Roman roads.

book:web_c366c13d.description: A Latin treatise on the nature of time, birthdays, and various chronological systems, written by the Roman grammarian Censorinus as a birthday gift for his patron Quintus Caerellius. It preserves valuable fragments of earlier Roman and Greek scholarship.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Censorinus's book as an authoritative source for dating historical events, though noting its limitations.

book:web_ee2ec2ab.description: A controversial philosophical work arguing for the degeneracy of the Americas and its indigenous peoples, influential in 18th-century European thought.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites De Pauw's philosophical research on the Americas for its data on walled towns.

book:web_112c45b2.description: A controversial two-volume comparative work by Dutch philosopher Cornelius de Pauw, arguing for the superiority of Chinese civilization over Egyptian, and containing speculative theories about both cultures that were debated in Enlightenment circles.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references this work for a discussion on fortifications and notes the anonymous author's (identified as De Pauw) familiarity with geography, while also quoting a critical judgment of De Pauw's methodology from M. Remusat.

book:web_8f1bfb90.description: A major 18th-century scholarly work on Roman Britain, compiling inscriptions, coins, and other antiquities. It was a foundational text for the study of Roman Britain for over a century.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Horsley's 'Britannia Romana' for details on Roman fortifications in Britain.

book:web_e72b0e0e.description: A major history of Spain by Jesuit scholar Juan de Mariana, originally published in Latin as 'Historiae de rebus Hispaniae' (often abbreviated 'Hist. Hispan.'). The cited 1733 Hague edition ('edit. Hag. Com. 1733') is a later collected edition of his works.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Mariana's historical work on Spain as a source for a ninth-century event and notes its stylistic imitation of Livy.

book:web_637f71fa.description: A work of universal history by the German historian Johann Christoph Gatterer, a prominent figure of the Göttingen School of History. The cited 1792 edition is the one referenced in Gibbon's text.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Gatterer's historical work to define the geographical boundaries of ancient Germany and the sources for its description.

book:web_07414bd9.description: A historical work by the church historian Johann Lorenz Mosheim examining the state of Christianity before Constantine the Great.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon praises Mosheim's work on Christian affairs before Constantine as a masterly performance and a key source for understanding the primitive church.

book:web_4cbc5366.description: A systematic theological defense of Quaker beliefs, often referred to as 'Barclay's Apology'. It was a foundational text for the Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) and argued for their principles by appealing to early Christian practices and scripture.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Barclay's work as defending Quaker principles by appealing to the authority of early Christian practices.

book:403447.description: A dramatic narrative of French history in the sixth century. Gregory of Tours (c.A.D. 539-594) intended his HISTORY to be a chronicle of events and included the 21 years he spent as Bishop of Tours. This volume contains all ten books of the HISTORY. As Gregory unravels the bewildering events of those decades, what emerges is no dry historical document but a colorful, detailed and moving pageant.
commentaries: Erich Auerbach directly references Gregory of Tours' historical work as the source for the subsequent narrative about Sicharius and Chramnesindus, presenting it as an example of raw historical material from the period.

book:web_bf878583.description: A standard work on ancient geography by Christoph Cellarius, frequently cited by 18th-19th century historians. The full title is often abbreviated as 'Geogr. Antiq.'
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Cellarius's work on ancient geography for information on the boundaries of Isauria.
Edward Gibbon cites Origen's work against Celsus as a source for early Christian doctrinal positions.

book:web_34332097.description: A treatise on ecclesiastical benefices and church-state relations, written by the Venetian theologian, historian, and statesman Paolo Sarpi (often called 'Fra Paolo'), best known for his opposition to papal authority. The work was published posthumously.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Fra Paolo's book alongside Prideaux's as a work to consult on the topic of tithes and benefices.

book:web_2eaefdfd.description: Commonly known as 'The Twelve Caesars', this work by Suetonius is a set of biographies of Julius Caesar and the first eleven Roman emperors.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Suetonius's biography of Tiberius for information on imperial cruelty and punishment.

book:1343276.description:
Con una introduccion de Jose Antonio Monge Marigorta, rescate de la excelente traduccion de las "Vidas de los doce cesares" de Suetonio hecha por F. Norberto Castilla directamente del latin y publicada por primera vez en 1883 en la "Biblioteca Clasica" de la editorial Hernando, de Madrid.
En este volumen se publica el Libro II de esta celebre obra, dedicado a Augusto. Con el proposito de facilitar la lectura, hemos adaptado ligeramente la traduccion a la ortografia moderna, actualizando la grafia de nombres...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Suetonius's biography of Augustus to support the claim that Augustus boasted of transforming Rome from brick to marble.

book:web_9eaeb9a0.description: A major work of historical geography by the renowned French cartographer d'Anville, compiling and critically assessing ancient geographical knowledge.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites D'Anville's geographical work to provide context about the location of Bostra.

book:web_b4bcea08.description: Posthumously published collection of d'Anville's geographical studies on medieval Europe, edited by his nephew. The work compiles his research on historical geography and was referenced by Gibbon for medieval place names and boundaries.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites d'Anville's work to support the etymology of the name Arragon from a local stream.

book:web_f475fafc.description: A geographical and historical treatise on ancient Gaul by the renowned French geographer and cartographer Jean-Baptiste Bourguignon d'Anville, published as part of his scholarly works on ancient geography.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references d'Anville's geographical work in a footnote discussing the provinces of Gaul.

book:web_b4d38c27.description: A historical chronology by Wilhelm Schickard, often cited in early modern scholarship. The reference to 'Rabbi Abraham' likely refers to Abraham ben David's chronicle, which Schickard included or discussed in his work.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Rabbi Abraham's historical chronicle regarding the persecution of Greeks.

book:web_4e9add55.description: Ovid's 'Fasti' is a six-book Latin poem on the Roman calendar, detailing religious festivals, astronomical events, and historical anniversaries. The work was composed around 8 CE and left unfinished due to Ovid's exile.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Ovid's work to provide a description of the festival of the Megalesia, noting its duration and the public celebrations.

book:web_56ce379c.description: A Latin treatise on the consecration of princes, likely referring to the German jurist and historian Johann Georg von Kulpis (also known as Vandale), who wrote on political and legal topics in the late 17th century.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Vandale's treatise, noting the difficulty of verifying its quotations.

book:web_99f65229.description: A collection of scholarly papers published by the French Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres. Nicolas Fréret (1688-1749) was a prominent French historian, antiquarian, and permanent secretary of the academy who contributed numerous memoirs to this publication series.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Freret's academic memoirs for a discussion on the probable Illyrian origin of the Italian Veneti.

book:web_4a8cea3c.description: A comprehensive numismatic lexicon (dictionary of coins) by German scholar Johann Heinrich Rasche, often abbreviated as 'Rasche, Lex. Univ. Ref. Numm.' in citations. It was a standard reference work for ancient coinage.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Rasche's universal lexicon on numismatics as a source for information on coins.

book:web_54695c27.description: Julius Caesar's firsthand account of the Gallic Wars, written as a series of commentaries. The work was composed during the war (c. 58–50 BCE) and circulated in Rome. The abbreviation 'de Bell. Gallic.' is a standard Latin reference to this classic historical and military text.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Caesar's commentary on the Gallic Wars as a primary historical source regarding the geography and limits of ancient Germany.
Edward Gibbon cites Caesar's 'De Bello Gallico' as a source for information about the Germans.
Edward Gibbon cites a specific book (VI) and chapter (23) of Caesar's 'de Bello Gallico' (The Gallic War) as a footnote reference for information on German warfare and territorial practices.

book:web_1a35453b.description: Julius Caesar's firsthand account of the Roman Civil War against Pompey and the Senate, covering events from 49-48 BCE. Written as a continuation of his Commentarii de Bello Gallico.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Caesar's own 'Commentaries' on the Civil War as a source for his actions in defense of tribunitian rights.

book:551328.description: In this volume are three works concerning the campaigns engaged in by the great Roman statesman Julius Caesar (10044 BCE), but not written by him. "The Alexandrian War, " which deals with troubles elsewhere also, may have been written by Aulus Hirtius (ca. 9043 BC, friend and military subordinate of Caesar), who is generally regarded as the author of the last book of Caesar's "Gallic War.""The African War" and "The Spanish War" are detailed accounts clearly by officers who had shared in the campaigns. All t...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Hirtius's work 'de Bello Alexandrino' for a description of Alexandria.

book:web_9fa01c10.description: A theological work by Bishop William Warburton arguing that the absence of explicit doctrine concerning the afterlife in the Mosaic law proves its divine origin, as no human legislator would have omitted such a necessary sanction.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon discusses Warburton's hypothesis concerning why the doctrine of immortality is omitted in the Mosaic law, noting its ingenuity and limited acceptance.

book:web_5332206f.description: A foundational work on the history of Christian church constitution by the German Protestant theologian and church historian.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon directs the reader to Plank's work on church constitution for further details on early church organization.

book:821682.description:
Dan Chiasson, hailed as "one of the most gifted poets of his generation" upon the appearance of his first book, takes inspiration for his stunning new collection from the Historia Naturalisof Pliny the Elder.
"What happens next, you won't believe," Chiasson writes in "From the Life of Gorky," and it is fair warning. This collection suggests that a person is like a world, full of mysteries and wonders-and equally in need of an encyclopedia, a compendium of everything known. The long title sequence offers ent...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Pliny's Natural History as an authentic and accurate source for details on provincial divisions and city conditions.
Edward Gibbon cites Pliny's 'Historia Naturalis' as a source regarding amber and fashion.
Edward Gibbon cites Pliny's 'Historia Naturalis' as a source for geographical or trade information.
Edward Gibbon cites Pliny's 'Historia Naturalis' as a source for financial estimates related to Indian trade.
Edward Gibbon cites Pliny's Natural History to provide information on the duties imposed on Indian commodities and the markup on their prices at Rome.
Edward Gibbon cites Pliny's Natural History as a source for information, referencing a specific book and chapter.
Edward Gibbon cites Pliny's Natural History as a source to confirm an idea about the early topography of Rome's hills.
Edward Gibbon cites Pliny's 'Historia Naturalis' as a source for geographical measurements and a description of Palmyra.
Edward Gibbon cites Pliny's Natural History as a source for information about the animals exhibited in Roman spectacles, referencing a specific book and chapter.
Edward Gibbon cites Pliny's Natural History for details on gold production from Spanish provinces and a silver mine in Dalmatia.

book:web_35b1fe22.description: A political oration (peri basileias) addressed to Emperor Arcadius, urging reform and stronger leadership against barbarian threats.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Synesius's book 'de Regno' as a source for the observation that Eastern provincials used the Greek title 'Basileus' (King) when addressing the Roman emperor.

book:web_ea6946e8.description: A Latin treatise on the origin and ancient seats of the Scythians, published in Bayer's collected works 'Opuscula' (Opuscula ad historiam antiquam, chronologiam, geographiam, et rem numariam spectantia). The citation refers to Bayer's discussion of Ephorus's division of the world among Scythians, Indians, Ethiopians, and Celts.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Bayer's work to trace the origin of the Greek division of the world's peoples to the historian Ephorus.

book:982243.description:
Edmund Curtis's remarkable survey of Ireland, from its earliest origins to the twentieth century, is a classic introduction to Ireland's fascinating history. Reaching from St Patrick's Mission in 432 to the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1922, this authoritative text explores the formative events of Ireland's past and encompasses the Norman invasion, Gaelic recovery, Cromwell's Settlement, the Act of Union, and the Great Famine.
Lucid and scholarly, this all-embracing account unfolds the events of Ireland's history....
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Keating's history as an example of a fanciful genealogical tradition used to trace Irish ancestry back to Noah, illustrating the 'rude superstructure of fable' built on Mosaic history.

book:web_dbe4d2bf.description: A geographical and political description of Greece by the ancient Greek philosopher and geographer Dicaearchus of Messana (c. 350–285 BCE). The work survives only in fragments, notably compiled in 'Geographi Graeci Minores' edited by Karl Müller (1855) and earlier in 'Geographiae Veteris Scriptores Graeci Minores' edited by John Hudson (1698–1712).
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Dicaearchus's work to support an observation about the modest simplicity of private houses in ancient Athens.

book:web_4dce5d17.description: An encyclopedic work covering natural history, astronomy, geography, medicine, art, and anthropology, written by Pliny the Elder and published around 77-79 AD. It is one of the largest single works to have survived from the Roman Empire.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Pliny's Natural History, noting a specific passage that was later interpreted by another scholar.
Edward Gibbon cites Pliny's Natural History as following the Augustan division of Italy.
Edward Gibbon references Pliny's Natural History for geographical description, linking it to other historical allusions.
Edward Gibbon references Pliny's Natural History as a source for the number of Roman colonies established in Spain.

book:550455.description: Pliny's Natural Historyis an astonishingly ambitious work that ranges from astronomy to art and from geography to zoology. Mingling acute observation with often wild speculation, it offers a fascinating view of the world as it was understood in the first century AD, whether describing the danger of diving for sponges, the first water-clock, or the use of asses' milk to remove wrinkles. Pliny himself died while investigating the volcanic eruption that destroyed Pompeii in AD 79, and the natural curiosity tha...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Pliny the Elder's 'Natural History' as an authority agreeing with the view that the Vandals and Goths were originally one people.

book:web_3f32d725.description: An epitome of the encyclopedic lexicon 'De verborum significatu' by Marcus Verrius Flaccus, compiled by Festus in the 2nd century AD. The work explains the meanings of obscure or archaic Latin words. Only about half of Festus's original text survives, preserved in a single damaged manuscript. Renaissance scholars produced important commentaries on this work.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Festus and his commentators for information on ancient Roman religious practices concerning places struck by lightning.

book:814393.description: Dionysius of Halicarnassus was born before 53 BCE and went to Italy before 29 BCE. He taught rhetoric in Rome while studying the Latin language, collecting material for a history of Rome, and writing. His "Roman Antiquities" began to appear in 7 BCE. Dionysius states that his objects in writing history were to please lovers of noble deeds and to repay the benefits he had enjoyed in Rome. But he wrote also to reconcile Greeks to Roman rule. Of the 20 books of "Roman Antiquities" (from the earliest times to 2...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites a specific volume and page from Dionysius Halicarnassus's work on Roman antiquities as a footnote reference.

book:web_3b89a684.description: A multi-volume ecclesiastical history and bibliography covering the first twelve centuries of Christianity, written by the French ecclesiastical historian Louis Ellies Dupin. The first volume was published in 1686, with subsequent volumes appearing over many years.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Dupin's ecclesiastical history as a source, likely regarding the church's rejection of Millennial doctrine.
Edward Gibbon cites Dupin's work as providing a detailed account of a specific dialogue composed by Methodius.

book:web_0f28af8f.description: A comprehensive history of Northern Europe by the German historian and statistician August Ludwig von Schlözer, covering the peoples and civilizations of Scandinavia, the Baltic region, and Russia.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Schlozer's opinion to critique the Greek geographical classification of barbarian peoples.

book:web_099dbe56.description: A pioneering work on Nordic history by the German historian and statistician August Ludwig von Schlözer, covering Scandinavian and northern European history.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Schlozer's theory that Runic characters are a corruption of the Roman alphabet.

book:web_2a7c2ba6.description: Massive encyclopedia of Islamic, Persian, Turkish, and other Eastern knowledge, compiled by French orientalist d'Herbelot. First major European reference work on Islamic civilization.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references D'Herbelot's work as a source on Artaxerxes' lineage, specifically the entry for Ardshir.

book:1268768.description: Lucan's great poem, Pharsalia, recounts events surrounding the decisive battle fought near Pharsalus in 48 B.C. during the civil war between the forces of Pompey and Julius Caesar. Though the subject of this unfinished masterpiece is historical, many of its features are characteristic of epic poetry: Rousing battle scenes; tales of witches, monsters, and miracle; detailed catalogues; intricate similes; and speeches with a high degree of rhetorical elegance. However, Lucan's deft mix of humor and horror, of....
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Lucan's epic poem 'Pharsalia' to illustrate the multifaceted and extraordinary character of Julius Caesar, describing a specific passage as a form of high praise.

book:web_29bb518a.description: A comprehensive history and description of New France (Canada) by Jesuit historian and explorer Charlevoix, often cited simply as 'Histoire du Canada'. The work is based on his travels and research in North America.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Charlevoix's history, likely as a comparative source, in a footnote.

book:web_38e3fb42.description: A comprehensive historical and topographical work on Alsace, written by the German historian and diplomat Johann Daniel Schoepflin. It was published in two volumes in 1751 and remains an important source for the history of the region.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon notes that the Abbé de la Bléterie's account of the wall is chiefly borrowed from Schoepflin's work.

book:web_682f2518.description: A two-volume work of ecclesiastical history by English theologian and historian John Jortin, containing critical remarks on early Christian history and the deaths of persecutors.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon mentions Dr. Jortin's work as an example of those who take pleasure in documenting the dramatic deaths of persecutors, before recommending a passage from Grotius.

book:web_b0ba42c9.description: A comprehensive historical and archaeological study of Verona and its antiquities, written by the Italian scholar and playwright Scipione Maffei. The work is notable for its systematic examination of Roman inscriptions, architecture, and history in the Verona region.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Maffei's work as providing a clear and comprehensive overview of Italy under the Roman emperors.
Edward Gibbon cites Maffei's work as an authoritative source that has examined the siege and battle of Verona with attention and accuracy.
Edward Gibbon cites Maffei's work on Verona in relation to the Etruscans and the early civilization of Italy.
Edward Gibbon lists Maffei's work as a consulted modern source.
Edward Gibbon references Maffei's work as an authority on the architectural details of the amphitheatre of Titus, using it to support descriptions of its structure and dimensions.

book:web_838eb633.description: A major scholarly work of Greek chronology by Henry Fynes Clinton, first published in 1824. It systematically organizes and dates events and figures from Greek history and literature.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Clinton's 'Fasti Hellenici' as a source providing population estimates for ancient Sparta.
Edward Gibbon cites Fynes Clinton's 'Essay in Fasti Hellenici' as a source on Athenian chronology.

book:web_3953b152.description: A concise history of Rome from its founding to the reign of Emperor Valens, written in Latin by the historian Eutropius in the 4th century AD. It was widely used as a school text in antiquity and the Middle Ages.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Eutropius's work to provide historical details about the character and policies of the emperor Constantius.

book:11334221.description: First published between 1880 and 1885, Joseph B. Mayor's three-volume edition of De Natura Deorum is remarkable for its thorough commentary. This volume contains Cicero's Book 2, which presents the Stoic argument for the existence of the gods and their providential ordering of the universe. Set within the home of the orator Caius Aurelius Cotta, it follows the Epicurean and Academic arguments of Book 1. Here the Stoic Balbus defends his basic premise that the majesty of creation - the harmony existing among...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon praises Cicero's 'De Natura Deorum' as the best guide to understanding the complex opinions of philosophers on the nature of the gods.

book:web_676d1644.description: A major work by French historian and statesman François Guizot, originally published as a series of lectures on modern European civilization from the fall of Rome to the French Revolution.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon quotes Guizot's interpretation of Tacitus's 'Germania' as a philosophical satire on Roman society.

book:web_c4a6ff50.description: A major work by French historian and statesman François Guizot, tracing the development of civilization in Europe. The first volume was published in 1829 as part of his lecture series at the Sorbonne.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Guizot's comparative analysis of ancient Germans and North American Indians.

book:web_c0313554.description: A comprehensive illustrated encyclopedia of classical antiquities by the French Benedictine monk and scholar Bernard de Montfaucon, published in multiple volumes between 1719-1724.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Montfaucon's work in the context of discussing the aqueducts and public works of the Roman empire.
Edward Gibbon references Montfaucon's work 'l'Antiquite Expliquee' as a source describing specific Roman bridges.

book:web_b43f8fe8.description: A geographical work by the Roman historian Arrian, describing a voyage around the Black Sea (Euxine Sea). It was written as a report to Emperor Hadrian around 131-132 AD, detailing coastal landmarks, distances, and Roman military installations.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Arrian's 'Periplus of the Euxine' for details on military garrisons and geography.

book:web_2d472d86.description: Multi-volume history of Roman emperors from Augustus to the 6th century AD, written by French ecclesiastical historian Tillemont. The work was published posthumously between 1690-1738 and was highly regarded for its meticulous scholarship and use of primary sources.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Tillemont's work as providing a clear resolution to chronological difficulties regarding Diocletian's abdication.
Edward Gibbon cites Tillemont's history as a source noting the doubtful and varied accounts of the war and death of Severus.

book:web_a7a20098.description: A scholarly work on Germanic runes by one of the Brothers Grimm, published in 1821.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon directs the reader to Grimm's work for further information on the high antiquity of Runic characters.

book:web_55c8b09c.description: A scholarly work on Jewish messianic expectations and Christology, written by German theologian Leonhard Bertholdt (1774-1822).
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Bertholdt's 'Christologia Judaeorum' as a source for understanding Jewish Messianic expectations.

book:8315520.description:
The "Saturnalia," Macrobius's encyclopedic celebration of Roman culture written in the early fifth century CE, has been prized since the Renaissance as a treasure trove of otherwise unattested lore. Cast in the form of a dialogue, the "Saturnalia" treats subjects as diverse as the divinity of the Sun and the quirks of human digestion while showcasing Virgil as the master of all human knowledge from diction and rhetoric to philosophy and religion.
The new Latin text is based on a refined understanding of the...
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Macrobius's 'Saturnalia' as a compilation, but comments that only a small portion relates to the title's theme.
Edward Gibbon cites Macrob's 'Saturnalia' as providing a specific form of evocation.

book:web_cf4e5637.description: A collection of diplomatic writings by Peter Patricius, a 6th-century Byzantine historian and diplomat. His works were preserved in the 'Excerpta de Legationibus' compiled under Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos in the 10th century.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Peter Patricius's work as a source for the narrative of Odenathus and Sapor.
Edward Gibbon cites Peter Patricius's work as a source for the conclusion of the military episode.

book:web_e127f217.description: A foundational work on the economic and administrative systems of ancient Athens, originally published in German as 'Die Staatshaushaltung der Athener'.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon references Boeckh's 'Public Economy of Athens' for a comparative analysis on Athenian citizen numbers.
Edward Gibbon cites Boeckh's book on the public economy of Athens as a source for information on Athenian population.

book:web_78ef3561.description: Historical work on Manchester by Reverend John Whitaker, first published in 1771, covering Roman and medieval periods of the city's history.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Whittaker's work as a source on the tribal divisions of ancient Britain.
Edward Gibbon references Whitaker's history as a source alongside Caesar for information on ancient fortifications.

book:web_f98cc3cf.description: A collection of agricultural essays by Walter Harte, an English poet and writer, focusing on farming practices including the cultivation of lucerne (alfalfa).
